papers.title: Stimulation strategy matters: A B-cell focused single-cell transcriptomic study on in vitro stimulated immune cells
papers.authors: D'hamers, T.; Neirinck, J.; Buysse, M.; De Vriendt, C.; Kerre, T.; Haerynck, F.; Hofmans, M.; Bonroy, C.; Everaert, C.
papers.abstract: Distinct in vitro B-cell stimulation strategies, defined by stimulation condition and incubation duration, have been described in diverse studies. Often, these approaches are considered interchangeable due to comparable flow-cytometric outputs concerning fluorescence intensities and B-cell subset distributions. However, whether these phenotypic similarities also reflect comparable underlying transcriptional states have not been systematically evaluated yet. In this study, we provide an unbiased comparison of B-cell activation strategies on healthy individuals, resulting in a single-cell transcriptomic atlas (4 donors; ~2,029 cells per sample; 81,160 cells in total with 56.3% annotated as B cells). Two T-cell independent stimulators targeting toll-like receptors (ODN2006 and IFN-{gamma}/R-848), were assessed next to two T-cell dependent stimulators (anti-CD40 and anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies), all incubated for eight and 30 hours. Observed overlap for differential abundance, differential gene expression and cell-cell interactions could directly be linked to T-cell (in)dependent working mechanism. Strategy-specific results uncovered time-point specific transcriptional changes, revealed the largest set of differentially expressed genes for IFN-{gamma}/R-848 and ODN2006, and showed that IFN-{gamma}/R-848 and anti-CD3/CD28 induced the majority of the cell-cell interactions. Ultimately, our reference atlas emphasizes the importance and facilitates the rational selection of optimal B-cell stimulation strategies, particularly for studies aiming to interrogate B-cell dysregulation in immune-mediated diseases.

papers.title: Regularized logistic regression-based gene selection for functional analysis of heterogeneous scRNA-seq macrophage populations in muscle aging and regeneration.
papers.authors: Costa, T. M.; Lopes, M. B.; Neves, J.; Sousa-Victor, P.; Vinga, S.
papers.abstract: Background: Single-cell RNA sequencing enables the characterization of heterogeneous cellular responses across experimental conditions. However, feature-selection methods often prioritize genes associated with global condition differences while overlooking subgroup-specific transcriptional structure. This limitation is particularly relevant in complex tissues, where distinct cell states may contribute differently to disease, aging, or regeneration. Regularized logistic regression provides an interpretable framework for sparse gene selection, but standard penalties do not explicitly account for differences in gene-gene correlation patterns across annotated subgroups. Results: We introduce DisTwiner, a subgroup-aware extension of the twiner correlation-based regularization framework for binary classification problems with multiple annotated groups. DisTwiner computes pairwise angular scores between feature-correlation profiles across subgroup labels and incorporates the resulting feature-specific weights into an Elastic Net-regularized logistic regression model. We evaluated DisTwiner using simulated data and a single-cell RNA-seq dataset of macrophage populations isolated from young and aged regenerating murine skeletal muscle. In simulated data, alternative aggregation and transformation strategies showed comparable classification performance, with minimum-based exponential weighting producing the greatest dispersion of feature penalties. In the macrophage dataset, DisTwiner achieved classification performance comparable to standard Elastic Net logistic regression and higher than Random Forest under the evaluated setting. Although predictive accuracy was similar to Elastic Net, DisTwiner selected genes with more heterogeneous fold-change and correlation patterns across macrophage subpopulations. Downstream enrichment analyses showed that DisTwiner-selected features captured biologically relevant aging-associated pathways, including interferon-response signatures in specific macrophage populations, and could serve as an additional filtering layer after differential expression analysis. Conclusions: DisTwiner extends correlation-based regularization to binary classification settings with multiple annotated subgroups, enabling feature selection that accounts for subgroup-specific correlation structure. Applied to single-cell macrophage data, the method preserved competitive classification performance while prioritizing genes with cell-population-dependent expression patterns, supporting its use for interpretable subgroup-aware feature selection in high-dimensional omics data.

papers.title: Functional single-cell omics in gynecological cancers immunotherapy: from heterogeneity dissection to clinical translation
papers.authors: Li D, Pei K, Yang B, Qie M, Xu J, Zhong L, Song L.

figure.label: Figure 1
figure.caption: Functional positioning and integrated application of single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is primarily employed for cell type annotation and classification. Single-cell epigenomic sequencing (scATAC-seq, scBS-seq, scRRBS, EM-seq) and scCUT&Tag are utilized for gene regulatory network (GRN) inference and assessment of cellular functional competence, respectively. Spatial transcriptomics integrates cellular identity with spatial location information, enabling the construction of cell–cell communication networks, identification of fine-scale subpopulations, and spatial dissection of tumor heterogeneity. Each individual omics modality offers a restricted view of biological complexity, and thus cannot comprehensively recapitulate intricate biological processes. In contrast, integrative analysis of multi-omics data enables the establishment of an “identity–state–space” tripartite analytical framework within the native tissue context, thereby facilitating systematic elucidation of the molecular mechanisms and spatial architecture underlying tumor heterogeneity.

papers.title: Disease-associated NK-cell state remodeling reveals transcriptional profiles predictive of clinical phenotypes
papers.authors: Meng, F.; Lin, P.; Zhang, S.; Li, T.; Liu, Z.; Ye, P.; Zhong, C.; Zhou, Y.
papers.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells adapt their cellular states to diverse tissue and inflammatory environments, yet how this plasticity manifests across pathological contexts and relates to patient-level disease phenotypes remains poorly defined. Here we established the Human NK-cell Atlas (HNKA) from over 1 million NK cells, including samples from 1,632 donors spanning 50 diseases. Within a shared NK-cell state architecture, analyses of state abundance and matched-reference exceedance distinguished disease-biased redistribution from transcriptional displacement. Fine-grained analyses localized disease-associated remodeling to specific NK-cell states, including CD56dim NK ISG15 in infection and autoimmunity and CD56bright NK ITM2C in tumors. These patterns were accompanied by recurrent interferon responses and state-specific regulatory activity. Cytokine perturbations recapitulated key transcriptional features of disease-associated NK-cell states. We developed NKceiver, a model based on state-specific NK-cell expression profiles for patient-level prediction. It distinguished 18 diseases and predicted COVID-19 severity and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, with predictive performance retained in unseen patients and studies. Collectively, our results reveal that disease-associated remodeling within the diverse NK-cell state repertoire resolved by HNKA is biologically interpretable and clinically informative, supporting disease discrimination and prediction of clinical phenotypes.

papers.title: Weaning imprints a hybrid cytotoxic-regulatory identity on intestinal CD4+ T lymphocytes
papers.authors: Schernthanner, M.; Gokhale, R.; Thoms, A.; dos Reis, G. L.; Saad, M.; Clark, M. M.; Yin, Y. S.; Mamede, I.; Reis, B. S.; Castro, T. B. R.; Parsa, R.; Fuchs, E.; Mucida, D.; Bilate, A. M.
papers.abstract: The intestinal immune system must adapt as the neonatal gut shifts from milk to solid food and becomes densely colonized. How the T cell compartment is established under these conditions remains unclear. Using fate-mapping to timestamp naive T cells, with imaging, transcriptomic, and repertoire analyses, we tracked them from suckling to adulthood. Intestinal T cell entry peaked at weaning, coinciding with relocation from crypts to villi guided by the tissue microenvironment and, partly, the microbiota. T cells timestamped at suckling persisted into adulthood and, at weaning, adopted a transient cytotoxic-regulatory state in the lamina propria, with granzyme B expression microbiota-dependent only in the ileum. Clonal expansions at weaning were restricted to the small intestinal lamina propria and absent in germ-free mice. Most expanded clones recognized early-life commensals. Weaning is a physiological window of transient inflammation imprinting a hybrid CD4 T cell compartment, suggesting that early-life commensals modulate T cell selection.

papers.title: An immune-inflammatory and thyroid function machine learning model for predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes: Development in a retrospective cohort and external validation in a prospective cohort.
papers.authors: Huang Y, Chen H, Xie X, Jin Y, Huang J.
papers.abstract: Objective Maternal thyroid dysfunction is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, yet thyroid status alone stratifies individual risk poorly and the immune-inflammatory contribution is rarely incorporated into prospectively validated prediction tools. We aimed to develop and externally validate a model predicting a composite adverse pregnancy outcome from antenatal thyroid and cytokine markers. Methods The model was developed in a retrospective cohort (n = 650; 131 events, 20.2%) and externally validated in an independent prospective cohort (n = 150; 26 events, 17.3%). Fifteen antenatal candidate predictors common to both cohorts were considered. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for variable selection; LASSO-logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting, and a support-vector machine were compared by repeated stratified cross-validation. Discrimination was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC); calibration and clinical utility were also assessed, with internal-external cross-validation (IECV) as a sensitivity analysis. Results LASSO retained three predictors: thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-10 (IL-10). LASSO-logistic regression was selected (development cross-validated AUC 0.762, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.692-0.846). On external validation, the model achieved an AUC of 0.750 (95% CI 0.647-0.848), exceeding a thyroid group-only reference model (AUC 0.625); the Brier score was 0.127, and the calibration slope was 1.77. Random 10-fold IECV gave a pooled AUC of 0.761 (95% CI 0.720-0.800). Higher IL-6 was associated with increased risk and higher IL-10 with decreased risk. Conclusion A parsimonious three-marker model combining TPOAb, IL-6, and IL-10 showed moderate discrimination for adverse pregnancy outcomes and outperformed thyroid status alone. Calibration requires refinement, and validation in larger multicenter cohorts is warranted before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Single-cell landscape of human adipose tissue reveals THBS1 as a potential driver of fibro-inflammation in metabolic disease.
papers.authors: Jung J, Park ES, Lee NK, Lee JJ, Juang U, Huang Q, Park YS, Kim HJ, Kim JK, Oh TJ, Suh JM, Kim JB, Moon JH, Kim JK, Choi SH.
papers.abstract: The cellular complexity of adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of metabolic disease; however, mechanisms underlying adipose dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we constructed a single-nucleus and bulk transcriptomic atlas of human visceral adipose tissues from an ethnically homogeneous cohort with defined metabolic states: lean with normal glucose tolerance, obesity, and obesity with type 2 diabetes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed a fibro-inflammatory subpopulation of adipose stem cells and adipocytes characterized by high THBS1 expression, which were enriched in individuals with obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes compared to lean controls. Through complementary in vitro (human primary ASCs, THP-1 macrophages, and Matrigel-captured mature adipocytes), ex vivo (mouse and human visceral adipose tissue explants), and in vivo (gain-of-function and antibody-mediated neutralization) experiments, we demonstrated that THBS1 promoted adipose fibrosis and inflammation via macrophage-mediated TGFβ activation, impairing adipogenesis and adipocyte function. Inhibition of THBS1 attenuated fibro-inflammatory features in metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissues. Moreover, THBS1 levels in plasma and adipocytes correlated with metabolic traits, including BMI and HbA1c. Collectively, our study provides a cellular atlas of human visceral adipose tissues across metabolic disease states and identifies THBS1 as a key pathogenic driver and potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Hypoxia-inducible CEA-targeted CAR T-cell therapy for relapsed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer.
papers.authors: Wei S, Guo J, Bai X, Zhou L, Mei Q, He S, Zhao J, Zhang S, Wang R, Cheng J, Su L, Liang L, Zhang L, Gong Y, Yu J, Feng H, Liu J, Yang X, Yang X, Yang X, Huang L, Wang L, Chen J, Shen J, Zhang Y, Zhang Y, Yang Z, Qian C, Tian W, Liu X, Wei J.
papers.abstract: Mitigating on-target off-tumor toxicity remains a central challenge for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for solid tumors. We developed a hypoxia-inducible CAR-T-cell product targeting carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) that restricts CAR activation to hypoxic tumor niches via oxygen-dependent expression control. In this first-in-human, phase I trial enrolling heavily pretreated patients with relapsed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), a single infusion of the investigational product achieved an objective response rate of 47% and a disease control rate of 87%, with a manageable safety profile. Exploratory analyses showed that clinical outcomes were associated with baseline factors. Deep single-cell profiling indicated that the clinical response was associated with the expansion of hypoxia-adapted, tumor-reactive-like CD8+ T cells alongside coordinated functional maturation of natural killer (NK) cells. Collectively, these data provide clinical proof-of-concept for hypoxia-inducible CAR design and inform the rational development of strategies leveraging tumor microenvironmental features in solid tumor cellular immunotherapy.

papers.title: ProtCell: a foundation model for single-cell proteomics
papers.authors: Hu, B.; Li, Z.; Jiang, Q.; Yin, Q.; Liu, Z.; Jiang, R.
papers.abstract: Single-cell proteomics provides a direct functional readout of cellular states, but targeted assays measure limited and non-identical protein panels, fragmenting information across experiments. Here, we present ProtCell, a foundation model developed using approximately 380 million cells from 98 datasets for pretraining and evaluation. ProtCell combines protein-identity and continuous-abundance embeddings in a transformer encoder and learns cell- and protein-level representations through masked abundance modeling. ProtCell first connects fragmented profiles through transferable annotation and batch correction while preserving biological organization. It then extends limited profiles through abundance reconstruction and inference of an unmeasured cytotoxic protein program enriched in natural killer cells and memory CD8$^+$ T cells. The learned protein dependencies further guide the selection of compact panels that retain information for profile reconstruction and biological classification. ProtCell thus provides a framework for connecting fragmented proteomic profiles, extending information beyond measured panels and guiding more informative measurements.

papers.title: Sensitivity and specificity of a rapid, point-of-care assay distinguishing bacterial from viral infections in acute care settings.
papers.authors: Sundaram ME, Wahlig TA, Arbefeville S.
papers.abstract: Differentiating between bacterial and viral infections is essential in the emergency department (ED) to guide appropriate antibiotic treatment. Recent assays, such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared MeMed BV assay, can help with this distinction. The MeMed BV assay measures three host immune proteins-Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-related apoptosis-induced ligand, Interferon (IFN)-γ-induced protein 10, and C-reactive protein-in blood samples. The results are combined into a score from 0 to 100, where a higher score indicates a higher likelihood of a bacterial infection and a lower score suggests a viral infection or other non-bacterial causes. The study evaluates the feasibility of using the MeMed BV assay-generated score to help clinicians decide whether to order blood cultures in emergency departments, as well as assessing the accuracy of the MeMed BV assay in distinguishing between bacterial and viral infections in ED patients. The assay's performance was also compared with standard biomarker tests and white blood cell (WBC) counts for predicting bacterial infections. This study included 203 illness episodes, of which a total of 108 were associated with bacterial infection (25 had a positive blood culture; 107 had a non-blood sample positive for a bacterial pathogen) and 18 were associated with a viral pathogen. Combined, the MeMed BV assay's "high bacterial likelihood" and "moderate bacterial likelihood" scores yielded a sensitivity and specificity of 87% and 32%, respectively, in correctly identifying any bacterial infection; the scores had a sensitivity and specificity of 95% and 25%, respectively, in correctly identifying bacteremia. The future of differentiating between bacterial and viral infections is moving toward integrated diagnostic methods. To address antibiotic resistance, future diagnostics will leverage host immune response biomarkers, advanced molecular panels, and machine learning techniques. This will enable rapid and accurate results at the point of care. Importance Distinguishing between bacterial and viral infections in healthcare settings can be challenging, as patients often present with similar symptoms and clinical features. In recent years, several new biomarkers have emerged as promising targets for algorithm-based tests designed to differentiate between these types of infections. An increasing number of FDA-approved assays that utilize these biomarkers have entered the market, employing various algorithms. These tests are being used in different clinical settings, such as emergency rooms, to assist clinicians in making accurate diagnoses and prescribing antibiotics appropriately. It is essential for clinicians to correctly order and interpret the results of these assays to fully realize their potential. Our study demonstrates that when such an assay is not used within the FDA-approved context, it does not achieve its full effectiveness.

papers.title: Analysis of the dynamic evolution and immunosuppressive functions of myeloid cells in gliomas based on single-cell transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Yuan H, Yang J, Bai Z, Wang H, Tong J, Chen P, Gong S.
papers.abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary brain tumor. However, the dynamic evolution of myeloid cells within its microenvironment and their role in immune suppression remain unclear. This study aims to elucidate the heterogeneity and immune regulatory mechanisms of myeloid cells, particularly tumor-associated neutrophils, through single-cell transcriptomic analysis. Methods We integrated single-cell transcriptomic data from 4 cases of GBM and 4 cases of low-grade glioma (LGG) to systematically analyze the myeloid cell landscape and identify neutrophil subpopulations and their differentiation trajectories. Utilizing CellChat cell-cell communication analysis, pseudotime trajectory analysis (performed on CD8 + T cells), and functional scoring, we revealed the interaction network between SRGN + neutrophils and CD8 + T cell subpopulations. Furthermore, based on the TCGA cohort, we constructed a SRGN + signature-based prognostic model to evaluate immune infiltration, immune checkpoints, TIDE immune evasion, and temozolomide sensitivity. Results Neutrophils were specifically enriched in GBM. A SRGN + subpopulation highly expressed S100A8/A9, IL1B, and PMN-MDSC-related genes, with elevated inflammation and S100 scores. Functional scoring indicated that this subpopulation exhibited pro-inflammatory and immunoregulatory characteristics. Among CD8 + T cells, three exhausted subsets were defined: Tex_PD1, Tex_NKG2A, and Tex_TIM3. CellChat-based ligand-receptor analysis predicted preferential chemotactic signaling from SRGN + neutrophils toward Tex_PD1 cells via CCL pathways and toward Tex_TIM3 cells via CXCL pathways, as well as potential inhibitory signaling toward Tex_NKG2A and Tex_TIM3 cells via the HLA-E-NKG2A axis. A 12-gene risk model stratified GBM patients into high- and low-risk groups. High-risk patients showed shorter overall survival but greater temozolomide sensitivity (reduced IC50 predicted by oncoPredict analysis), alongside an immune phenotype of "increased T-cell infiltration yet functional exhaustion." TIDE analysis confirmed elevated dysfunction scores, reduced exclusion scores, and low MDSC phenotype scores, consistent with SRGN + neutrophils lacking classic MDSC markers. Conclusion This study systematically characterizes the dynamic evolution and immunosuppressive functions of myeloid cells, particularly SRGN + neutrophils, in GBM, suggesting a potential dual "chemotactic recruitment and selective suppression" mechanism by which they may shape the landscape of CD8 + T-cell exhaustion. The risk model constructed based on this subpopulation demonstrated prognostic stratification value within the TCGA-GBM cohort, pending validation in independent cohorts, and suggests a potential therapeutic strategy combining targeting of the HLA-E-NKG2A axis with temozolomide.

papers.title: Integrated Multiomics and Functional Validation Identify CLSPN as a Central Integrator of Genomic Instability and Immune Remodeling in Colorectal Cancer.
papers.authors: Wang P, Xia J, Wang L, Hu B, Jiang H, Wang X, Fang X, Liu X, Zhao X, Li X.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is characterized by pervasive genomic instability, yet the molecular mechanisms linking replication stress responses to genome alteration and phenotypic evolution remain incompletely understood. Here, we performed an integrative multiomics analysis combined with functional validation to investigate the role of CLSPN, a key adaptor of the ATR-CHK1 pathway, in CRC. Machine learning-based feature selection identified CLSPN as a robust prognostic factor. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses revealed that CLSPN is preferentially enriched in highly proliferative tumor cell populations and spatially localized within tumor core regions. Elevated CLSPN expression was strongly associated with increased copy number variation burden (FGA, FGG, and FGL) and chromosomal instability, indicating enhanced tolerance to replication stress and accumulation of genomic alterations. This genomic instability was further linked to remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. Functional assays demonstrated that CLSPN promotes proliferation, invasion, and migration while suppressing apoptosis in CRC cells. Collectively, these findings identify CLSPN as a key regulator of replication stress-driven genomic instability and highlight its role in shaping mutation-associated tumor evolution, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Single-cell analysis of COPD: Microenvironmental interactions driven by immune-fibrotic imbalance.
papers.authors: Jiang H, Wang W, Wang L, Wu J, Luo J, Yan Q, Gong X, Liang J.
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a respiratory disease with a high degree of cellular heterogeneity and molecular complexity, characterized pathologically by persistent airflow limitation and an inflammatory-tissue remodeling cascade involving multiple cell types. Traditional transcriptomics lack the resolution to precisely define cell subpopulation roles in COPD. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) overcomes this limitation by enabling high-resolution analysis of cell-type-specific mechanisms in COPD. A total of 101,009 cells from three scRNA-seq datasets were integrated to profile COPD-related molecular features and cell interactions at single-cell resolution. Analysis identified four major cell types and 17 distinct cell subtypes. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed a significant reduction in signaling activity of macrophages and fibroblasts, whereas certain immune cells exhibited enhanced signaling, suggesting that immune dysregulation plays a pivotal role in COPD pathogenesis. Further analysis focused on macrophage-dominant myeloid cells and fibroblasts, uncovering their critical roles in inflammation modulation and fibrosis progression. Meanwhile, this study also identified 19 chemicals that may influence COPD progression by modulating cellular gene expression. This study provides an important molecular basis for unraveling the cell-cell interaction network of COPD and elucidating the mechanism of each cell subpopulation in the disease process.

papers.title: A PTN+ glioblastoma subclone orchestrates immune reprogramming to drive distant recurrence.
papers.authors: Yan X, Hu J, Hu Y, Xu M, Gao S, Han X, Zhao D, Li Q, Zhou L, Hu S.
papers.abstract: Aims Distant recurrence (DR) represents a distinct and lethal trajectory in glioblastoma (GBM), characterized by the colonization of spatially isolated neural niches. The mechanisms by which disseminated tumor cells remodel the microenvironment to overcome anatomical and immunological barriers remain poorly understood. This study aimed to decode the immune ecosystem of DR and elucidate the intercellular crosstalk driving this lethal dissemination. Methods We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on paired primary and DR tumor specimens from GBM patients, alongside an independent local recurrence (LR) control cohort, to map dynamic cellular shifts. Bioinformatic analyses, including differential abundance testing (Milo), cell-cell communication inference (CellChat), and copy number variation (CNV) analysis, were integrated with clinical co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) validation, bidirectional in vitro co-culture assays, and an orthotopic xenograft mouse model. Results Our high-resolution atlas revealed a profound remodeling of the microenvironment in DR lesions, characterized by a specific expansion of anti-inflammatory monocyte-derived tumor-associated macrophages (Anti_infl-TAM) and a paradoxical co-enrichment of CD8 + T cells and Tregs. Mechanistically, an OPC-like subpopulation of PTN+ tumor cells acted as a "paracrine architect," promoting Anti_infl-TAM polarization through the interaction between PTN and NCL. Co-IP assays confirmed direct physical binding of these two proteins in human DR tissues. Functional and bidirectional knockdown assays demonstrated that decoupling this cellular communication, achieved by targeting either PTN in tumor cells or NCL in macrophages, significantly attenuated glioma cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and macrophage polarization. In vivo, silencing PTN markedly reduced Anti_infl-TAM infiltration, suppressed intracranial tumor burden, and prolonged overall survival in tumor-bearing mice. Conclusion This study establishes that DR GBM is defined by a reconfigured immune niche rather than mere genetic drift. The paracrine crosstalk between PTN+ tumor cells and Anti_infl-TAM serves as a critical engine of this permissive soil, offering a promising therapeutic target to disrupt the supportive microenvironment in distant recurrent GBM.

papers.title: Combining Single-Cell Data with Machine Learning Uncovers the Molecular Landscape of Keratoconus.
papers.authors: Fang X, Han P, Chen S, Zhang J, Hua X, Chen P.
papers.abstract: Purpose Keratoconus (KC) is a progressive disorder characterized by corneal ectasia, corneal thinning, and conical protrusion, which can lead to diminished vision and corneal scarring. However, the molecular mechanism underlying KC has not yet been fully elucidated. In this study, we combined bioinformatics tools and experimental assays to uncover cell-type-specific pathogenic regulators and promising diagnostic biomarkers of KC. Methods We analyzed the KC-associated bulk mRNA expression dataset GSE151631 (19 KC, 7 controls) and the single-cell RNA sequencing dataset GSE285060 (5 KC, 3 controls) from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. After quality control, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and annotation of single cells, we assessed each subpopulation's role in the disease and conducted differential expression analysis on the most relevant subpopulation. Feature selection was then performed on the bulk RNA-seq dataset using LASSO regression and SVM-RFE algorithms to identify candidate diagnostic genes. As a preliminary in vivo validation, an acute rabbit model of KC was induced by intrastromal injection of collagenase type II, and corneal tissues were harvested at day 7 to assess key gene expression at mRNA and protein levels by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence, respectively. We also performed immune infiltration analysis, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA), transcriptional regulatory networks construction, pseudotime trajectory analysis, and connectivity map (cMap)-based drug prediction. Results Corneal stromal cells exhibited the highest contribution to the disease state. Three key genes (KIAA0930, CCDC85B, and KLHL21) were identified as potential diagnostic biomarkers. Notably, KIAA0930 was upregulated in the rabbit KC model, while CCDC85B and KLHL21 were downregulated, consistent with bioinformatic analysis. Immune infiltration analysis indicated increased cytolytic activity and CD8 + T cells in KC samples, with key genes showing significant correlations with various immune cell types and factors. GSEA and GSVA analyses revealed that these three genes are linked to ECM-receptor interaction, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, and WNT/β-catenin signaling pathways. Pseudotime analysis revealed distinct transcriptional states between KC and control cells. Several small-molecule compounds, including menadione and PAC-1, were computationally predicted to show negative connectivity with the KC-associated gene expression signature. Conclusions Our study identifies KIAA0930, CCDC85B, and KLHL21 as promising candidate biomarkers for KC diagnosis and highlights corneal stromal cells as a central contributor to KC pathological progression. By combining single-cell transcriptomics and machine learning with preliminary validation in an acute rabbit model, this work provides a molecular framework for early KC diagnosis and therapy, pending validation in chronic models and human cohorts.

papers.title: Machine learning dataset and benchmark for accurate T cell receptor-pHLA binding prediction.
papers.authors: Zhu X, Lu J, Lu Y, Zhang Y, Feng F.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in immunology and therapeutic design is accurately predicting the diverse interactions between T cell receptors and peptide-human leukocyte antigen (pHLA) complexes. Existing machine learning tools are hindered by incomplete sequence data and biased nonbinding examples. Here we present Hi-TPH, a large-scale hierarchical dataset featuring an on-the-fly selection method for generating nonbinding data. We further develop Hi-TPH-PLMs, a collection of protein language models (PLMs) with varied architectures and scales, fine-tuned on Hi-TPH. These models achieve a 19.2% performance gain over state-of-the-art tools on an external wet-lab test set. Leveraging the hierarchical structure of Hi-TPH, detailed analyses dissect the contribution of different molecular components to binding prediction and reveal their synergistic interplay; for instance, the prediction contribution of HLA relies on the presence of full T cell receptor chains. Hi-TPH and Hi-TPH-PLMs are publicly released to support the development of more reliable tools for advanced immunoinformatics research and personalized immunotherapy.

papers.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts and immune evasion in endometrial cancer: current evidence and therapeutic perspectives.
papers.authors: Zhan J, Yan Z, Cao Z, Wu F, Wang Y, Zhan Y.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are potential contributors to tumor progression and immune resistance in endometrial cancer (EC), but the extent of EC-specific mechanistic and therapeutic evidence remains uneven. Studies using EC-derived fibroblasts support tumor-promoting paracrine activity and provide experimental evidence of altered natural killer cell function. Single-cell and spatial analyses further characterize stromal heterogeneity and candidate intercellular interactions. However, many proposed mechanisms of CAF-mediated immune exclusion and most CAF-directed therapeutic strategies are informed by studies in other malignancies. This review distinguishes findings obtained in EC patient samples and experimental models from evidence extrapolated from pancreatic, breast, gastric, and other cancers. We examine CAF heterogeneity, soluble signaling, matrix remodeling, and immune-cell interactions, while identifying where functional validation in EC is still required. Therapeutic approaches, including FAP-directed interventions, stromal reprogramming, and signaling blockade combined with immune checkpoint inhibition, are discussed as candidate research strategies rather than established EC treatments. Priorities include validating CAF-immune mechanisms in EC, developing reproducible stromal biomarkers, and testing treatment combinations in appropriate disease-specific models and clinical studies.

papers.title: Intestinal Candida albicans promotes HCC progression and anti-PD-1 resistance via IL-17A and Trem2 + macrophages.
papers.authors: Zhang L, Wang K, Chai D, Mo T, Jiang W, Ma W, Yu B, Shi Q, Ding P, Deng W, Wang W, Zhao K, Chen C.
papers.abstract: Background & aims Whether intestinal fungal dysbiosis contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) remains unclear. We investigated how gut Candida albicans influences HCC progression, immune remodeling, and response to ICI therapy. Methods Fecal and tumor samples from patients with HCC, liver cirrhosis, and healthy controls were analyzed using ITS2 sequencing, immune profiling, and correlation analyses. Mechanistic studies focused on four complementary autochthonous murine HCC models and cell-based assays, integrating single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing, genetic and pharmacologic perturbations, Kaede photoconversion, fungal antigen recall assays, antifungal treatment, and anti-PD-1 therapy. Results Fecal C. albicans abundance was higher in HCC patients and was associated with advanced disease, shorter overall survival, and reduced durable clinical benefit. Across HCC models, C. albicans gavage increased tumor burden and induced a Th17/IL-17A-skewed microenvironment characterized by Trem2 + macrophage accumulation and impaired CD8 + T cell infiltration and function. Antifungal treatment attenuated tumor progression, whereas IL-17A blockade or deficiency largely abrogated C. albicans-associated tumor promotion. Mechanistically, IL-17A induced tumor-derived MCP-1 through ACT1-TRAF6-TAK1 signaling to recruit macrophages and upregulated PAI-1, which activated TGF-β/Smad3 signaling to promote an immunosuppressive Trem2 + macrophage state. These macrophages limited CD8 + T cell recruitment and effector function through coordinated CXCL10 repression and GAL-1 induction, while potentially reinforcing Th17 responses through IL-1β and IL-6. Kaede photoconversion demonstrated enhanced mesenteric lymph node-to-liver Th17 trafficking, while fungal antigen recall assays revealed preferential Th17 responsiveness to C. albicans. C. albicans also impaired anti-PD-1 efficacy in vivo, whereas antifungal treatment partially restored therapeutic responsiveness. Conclusions Intestinal C. albicans promotes HCC progression and anti-PD-1 resistance through an IL-17A-Trem2 + macrophage circuit, supporting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target. Impact and implications Intestinal fungal dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a component of the gut-liver axis, but its functional contribution to HCC has remained poorly defined. Our study identifies intestinal Candida albicans as a promoter of HCC progression in experimental models and delineates an IL-17A-MCP-1/PAI-1-Trem2 + macrophage circuit that links fungal exposure to impaired CD8 + T-cell immunity and reduced response to PD-1 blockade. These findings are relevant to researchers and clinicians seeking microbiome-associated determinants of HCC progression and immunotherapy resistance. Fecal C. albicans abundance and components of this immune circuit may warrant evaluation as biomarkers for patient stratification and as potential targets for combination therapy. However, the clinical associations reported here are based on modest observational cohorts, and antifungal treatment was tested as a proof-of-concept intervention in mice. Larger prospective studies and more selective therapeutic approaches will therefore be required before these findings can inform clinical management.

papers.title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis of ferroptosis-related programs in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.
papers.authors: Fu F, Zhang D, Zhuang S, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Background High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) shows marked molecular and microenvironmental heterogeneity. How ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs) relate to immune and metabolic states across bulk tumors and single cells is incompletely defined. Methods We analyzed TCGA-OV RNA-seq data from 421 patients (419 evaluable for survival) using a curated 25-gene FRG panel, assessing expression, co-expression, survival, and immune/checkpoint associations. Single-cell data from GSE300897 (nine treatment-naive HGSOC donors; 16,939 cells after QC) scored FRG and pathway activity across nine subtypes and compared chemo-refractory versus chemo-sensitive tumors by donor-level pseudobulk analysis. Results FTL, FTH1, RPL8, and LDHA were among the most highly expressed FRGs; inter-gene coordination was modest. The aggregate FRG score was not prognostic (log-rank p = 0.80; AUCs 0.52, 0.54, 0.46 at 1, 3, 5 years) but correlated with cytotoxic, CD8 T-cell, macrophage, and Treg signatures. At single-cell resolution, the FRG score was highest in myeloid cells, with enriched iron-metabolism gene expression. Refractory tumors showed higher myeloid and lower fibroblast/plasma-cell fractions, and malignant cells showed directional increases in GLS, CS, and TFRC with decreases in SLC7A11, HMOX1, and GPX4 (none surviving correction). The FRG score showed reproducible positive coupling with hypoxia, glycolysis, and NF-κB programs across platforms. qRT-PCR confirmed higher FTH1, FTL, GPX4, and SLC7A11 in SKOV3 and OVCAR3 versus IOSE80 cells. Conclusions Ferroptosis-related transcriptional programs in HGSOC are cell-type dependent and associate with immune infiltration and selected inflammatory/metabolic states, without independent prognostic value. These findings nominate myeloid iron-handling and antioxidant shifts in malignant cells as testable hypotheses for future validation.

papers.title: Single-Cell Atlas of Human Orthodontic Tooth Movement.
papers.authors: Zhao W, Wu S, Lin Y, Zhang K, Xu H, Jin Z, Sun X, Gu H, Yang P, Song A, Sun W, Zhang H, Yan B.
papers.abstract: Orthodontic tooth movement (OTM) requires coordinated remodeling of the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, but the cellular architecture underlying this process in human tissues remains incompletely understood. We generated the first single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the human periodontal ligament during OTM by profiling control tissues and pressure- and tension-side tissues collected at days 3 and 7 following force application. Analysis of 65,032 cells identified 15 cell populations and revealed pronounced remodeling of stromal, immune, vascular, and neural compartments that varied by force direction and stage. Within the fibroblast compartment, we identified a CTHRC1 + fibroblast subset that was enriched on the pressure side at day 3 and exhibited heightened mechanotransduction, inflammatory signaling, and chemokine programs. TRPA1 was preferentially expressed in this subset, and computational perturbation, tissue validation, and pharmacologic inhibition supported its involvement in early remodeling on the pressure side. Ligand-receptor and functional analyses further implicated C3 as a downstream remodeling mediator linking regions rich in CTHRC1 + fibroblasts to monocyte recruitment and osteoclastogenic activity. In a mouse OTM model, systemic treatment with HC-030031 and local Trpa1 knockdown mediated by AAV9 under the Postn promoter reduced tooth movement, while HC-030031 also decreased osteoclast surface. Local C3a supplementation partially restored tooth movement during TRPA1 inhibition. These intervention data, with in vitro assays and tissue validation, support the involvement of TRPA1-associated signaling in a pressure-responsive stromal remodeling program and C3 as a potential downstream mediator of osteoclastogenic remodeling. These findings provide a human single-cell framework for periodontal remodeling during OTM and identify a pressure-responsive CTHRC1 + fibroblast population in which mechanosensitive TRPA1 contributes to osteoclastogenic remodeling on the pressure side.

papers.title: Blocking aryl hydrocarbon receptor remodels myeloid-T cell crosstalk and enhances anti-PD-1 response in the tumor microenvironment.
papers.authors: Kim DK, Baek S, Kim Y, Yang SM, Park SY, Choi SJ, Lee JH, Lee SH, Cho J, Cha D, Kim D, Kim S, Kim JH, Cho BC.
papers.abstract: Purpose Cancer metabolism-associated immune suppression remains a major barrier to durable therapeutic responses. Indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase 1 has been pursued as a therapeutic target, but incomplete pathway suppression has limited clinical success. As the aryl hydrocarbon receptor is a ligand-activated transcription factor and downstream effector of tryptophan metabolism, we investigated how myeloid-cell aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling shapes the tumor immune microenvironment and whether its inhibition can restore antitumor immunity. Methods Conditional aryl hydrocarbon receptor knockout mice targeting dendritic cells or macrophages were used to evaluate the effects of genetic aryl hydrocarbon receptor ablation. Pharmacologic inhibition was assessed using DA-4505 across syngeneic lung, colorectal, and breast cancer models and an immune checkpoint inhibitor-refractory humanized patient-derived xenograft model. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated alone or in combination with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 therapy, chemotherapy, or surgery. Tumor growth, survival, metastasis, and immune remodeling were analyzed by flow cytometry, multiplex immunohistochemistry, single-cell RNA sequencing, cytokine profiling, and human tumor datasets. Results Conditional aryl hydrocarbon receptor depletion in macrophages and dendritic cells enhanced innate and adaptive immune activation, increased interferon-γ-producing T cells, and strengthened antitumor immunity. In mouse tumor models, pharmacologic aryl hydrocarbon receptor blockade enhanced macrophage chemotaxis and activation programs, promoted M1-like macrophage polarization, increased interferon-γ-producing CD8⁺ T cells, and reduced regulatory T cells and polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells. These changes promoted robust T-cell activation and durable tumor control. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor inhibition further synergized with chemotherapy, surgery, and immune checkpoint blockade, leading to expansion of effector and memory T-cell populations and sustained antitumor responses. In a humanized lung cancer model, aryl hydrocarbon receptor blockade increased intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and cytotoxic-memory programs while reducing regulatory T-cell enrichment. In human tumor datasets, aryl hydrocarbon receptor-positive macrophages correlated with FOXP3⁺ T-cell infiltration, and higher aryl hydrocarbon receptor inhibition-associated T-cell signatures were associated with improved patient survival.

papers.title: RNF152 inhibits immune evasion in clear cell renal cell carcinoma by promoting the ubiquitination of PD-L1.
papers.authors: Wang Q, Liu YR, Zhu XB, Peng JC, Chen S.
papers.abstract: Dysregulation of ubiquitination drives tumor progression in various cancers, including clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). RING finger protein 152 (RNF152) is a ubiquitin E3 ligase that regulates cancer development. This study aimed to investigate the role of RNF152 in ccRCC and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanism. RNF152 expression and its correlation with survival were analyzed through bioinformatics analysis of the RNA expression profile from TCGA. Tumor cell viability and colony formation, as well as cytotoxicity of co-cultured CD8 + T cells, were assessed. Tumor growth and immune evasion were evaluated using a tumor-bearing mouse model. Furthermore, whether RNF152 regulates PD-L1 via ubiquitination was investigated. RNF152 was expressed at low levels in ccRCC, and high RNF152 expression correlated with better patient survival. Overexpression of RNF152 inhibited proliferation and immune evasion of ccRCC cells in vitro, while knockdown of RNF152 had the opposite effects. Moreover, RNF152 promoted degradation of PD-L1 by facilitating K48-linked polyubiquitination, and the ubiquitination site was identified as K64. Additionally, overexpression of PD-L1 counteracted the inhibition of proliferation and immune evasion induced by RNF152. In vivo, anti-PD-L1 therapy inhibited tumor growth and immune evasion in mice with RNF152 knockdown. facilitating ubiquitination of PD-L1. These findings reveal a novel regulatory mechanism in ccRCC and highlight the therapeutic potential of upregulating RNF152 to enhance anti-tumor immunity, potentially in combination with anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy.

papers.title: Aurora-A promotes tumor progression and remodels the Th2-associated immune microenvironment.
papers.authors: Yan W, Xie Z, Chen X, Hu L, Guo H, Wang C, Li Y, Li R, Hu B, Liu Q, Chen W, Sun J, Wang Q, Ren J, Li H.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to elucidate the critical role and molecular mechanisms of Aurora-A in the malignant progression and immune microenvironment remodeling of glioblastoma (GBM). Aurora-A is abnormally overexpressed in GBM and is associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and poor patient prognosis. This study demonstrates that high AURKA expression correlates with adverse molecular subtypes (IDH wild-type, 1p/19q non-codeletion) and serves as an independent prognostic risk factor. Functional assays revealed that knockdown of AURKA significantly inhibits the proliferation and migration of GBM cells. Bioinformatics analysis linked AURKA expression to specific immune infiltration patterns, showing a strong positive correlation with inferred Th2 cell infiltration and a negative correlation with CD8⁺ T cell presence. AURKA knockdown not only inhibited tumor growth but also significantly reduced the expression of Th2-related cytokines and the infiltration of CD4⁺ T cells within the tumor. Mechanistically, Aurora-A activates the NF-κB pathway, leading to upregulation of the Th2-recruiting chemokines CCL22 and CCL17. Recruited Th2-skewed CD4+ T cells secrete IL-4 and IL-13, which in turn promote glioma cell proliferation via the JAK1/STAT6 signaling pathway. This establishes a positive feedback loop that drives tumor progression and immune microenvironment remodeling. These findings reveal a novel non-cell-autonomous role for Aurora-A in promoting an immunosuppressive Th2-skewed microenvironment, providing a rationale for combining Aurora-A inhibitors with immunotherapy to enhance anti-tumor efficacy in GBM.

papers.title: Machine learning classification of fibromyalgia from blood transcriptomes: confounder benchmarking and implications for endometriosis-associated pain
papers.authors: Ouni, S.; Ouni, F.; Chebbi, A.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia (FM) lacks an objective biomarker, and blood transcriptomic signatures have been proposed to fill this gap. Here, the largest public peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) RNA-seq cohort of FM reporting expression subtypes (96 patients, 93 controls) was reanalysed using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection and scaling confined strictly to training folds. Gene expression discriminated patients from controls (ROC-AUC 0.821 for logistic regression and 0.825 for XGBoost), clearing a 100-repetition permutation-label null (p= 0.0099). Two simple, disease-agnostic baselines, however, reach nearly the same performance: sex alone reaches AUC 0.727, and a four-score PBMC cell-composition proxy reaches AUC 0.71-0.76. Restricting to females alone gives AUC 0.783 (0.705-0.858), and excluding X/Y-linked genes does not reduce performance, so the signal is not purely a sex-composition artifact; but the female-only expression model does not significantly exceed the composition-only proxy in the same females (0.783 vs. 0.712, paired 95% CI -0.025 to 0.175), so a composition contribution cannot be excluded. Preranked gene set enrichment analysis finds curated CLEAR/lysosomal and interferon/JAK-STAT gene sets, proxies for two subtype signatures of the original study, enriched among genes expressed lower in FM, also in females alone, but this enrichment disappears after adjusting for the composition proxies. Gynecological comorbidity, hormonal status, and medication are absent from the public metadata and remain plausible, untested contributors to the female-only estimate. These findings are hypothesis-generating, not a basis for clinical diagnosis: a single-cohort, correlational result consistent with, but not sufficient to establish, an FM-specific signal distinct from demographic, hormonal, and cell-composition confounds, pending independent replication. Future blood-based biomarker studies for FM, and for related nociplastic pain conditions such as endometriosis, should report performance relative to sex- and composition-based baselines as standard practice.

papers.title: A microbiome-reactive TMIGD2 hi Th17 subset is spatially enriched at the intestinal epithelium and expanded in inflammatory bowel disease.
papers.authors: Pedersen TK, Jain T, Segerstolpe Å, Lin C, Shih AR, Yuan L, Ashenberg O, Kaper ME, Twardus SW, Ricciardi R, Lau H, Moon JJ, Brix S, Xavier RJ, Graham DB.
papers.abstract: Subsets of intestinal CD4 + T cells directly recognize commensal bacteria and coordinate tolerance versus protective immunity. Our limited understanding of CD4 + T cell specificities and corresponding functional phenotypes has created a barrier to deciphering the mechanisms of mucosal homeostasis and inflammation mediated by the adaptive immune system. To address this, we leveraged an immunodominant Bacteroidetes epitope in SusC to perform single-cell profiling of the SusC-specific and total CD4 + T cell landscapes in intestinal tissues of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). By analyzing phenotypes and T cell receptor specificities in parallel, we uncovered phenotypic diversification of T helper 17 (Th17) cells in IBD and identified an epithelial-localized, SusC-reactive Th17 subset that is BACH2 lo , GZMA hi , and expresses the costimulatory receptor TMIGD2. Together, our results highlight the utility of tracking commensal-specific T cell responses to define specialized subsets of Th17 cells associated with loss of tolerance to the microbiome.

papers.title: An Explainable Multimodal Deep-Learning Model Using Histopathological Image and Clinical Information for Prognosis Prediction in Colorectal Cancer: A Multi-Center Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Jiang Z, Shi X, Su C, Ma Y, Li R, Chen M, Cui J, Hawkins N, Ward R, Bai X, Jonnagaddala J, Fu W, Zhou X.
papers.abstract: Accurate prognostication is crucial for the individualized management of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), while the accuracy and interpretability of current models still need to be improved. This study aims to develop and validate an explainable multimodal model for precise survival prediction. 3381 patients with resected CRC are enrolled from three medical centers, and a multimodal deep-learning framework integrating clinical variables and histopathological images is developed. The multimodal model exhibits significantly more robust performance than unimodal models in prognosis prediction across all of the cohorts. By stratifying patients into low-risk and high-risk groups based on the model-derived risk scores, high-risk patients exhibit worse outcomes, and the stratification remains an independent prognostic factor in multivariable Cox regression. The model also identifies patients with markedly poorer survival among the stage II/III subgroup. Adjuvant chemotherapy demonstrates benefits in high-risk patients with stage III CRC but not in the low-risk group. Multi-omic analyses disclose that low-risk tumors are characterized by enhanced adaptive immune responses, whereas high-risk tumors exhibit stronger angiogenesis and higher exhaustion scores of T cells, reflecting a hypoxic and immunosuppressive microenvironment. These results support the potential of the multimodal model to effectively predict survival outcomes in resected CRC with great explainability.

papers.title: Unraveling novel bioactive phytoconstituents from Annona squamosa L. and their mechanisms of action for the relief from rheumatoid arthritis: an integrated network pharmacology, docking and MD simulations approach.
papers.authors: Alam MJ, Morshed MR, Chowdhury MH, Hossain S, Hena H.
papers.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease marked by synovial inflammation, gradual joint deterioration, and extra-articular complications, resulting from a complex interplay of genetic predispositions, immune system dysregulations, and environmental factors. Synthetic medicines provide symptomatic relief but have significant side effects, limited long-term efficacy, and high costs, highlighting the need for safer and more effective multi-target therapies. Plant-derived compounds represent promising candidates for the development of novel multi-target therapeutic agents for immune-mediated and inflammatory disorders such as RA. Our study employed network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to investigate the therapeutic effects of bioactive phytocompounds from Annona squamosa L. on RA. Bioactive phytocompounds were retrieved via systematic screening of curated databases and literature mining, followed by ADMET profiling and drug-likeness assessment. The putative targets of A. squamosa phytocompounds and RA-associated genes were identified via SwissTargetPrediction and GeneCards, respectively. Protein-protein interaction network (PPIN) analysis identified ten critical hub target genes, while Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses demonstrated biological processes associated with RA pathogenesis and key signaling pathways. Four bioactive phytocompounds-quercetin, luteolin, isorhamnetin, and kaempferol-were predicted to inertact with 98 potential molecular targets, of which 50 corresponded to targets associated with RA. Ten hub target genes were identified: AKT1 , EGFR , SRC , MMP9 , GSK3B , PARP1 , MMP2 , IGF1R , KDR , and MET . Pathway enrichment analysis revealed the focal adhesion and Rap1 signaling pathways as significantly involved, alongside other biologically enriched pathways. The molecular docking demonstrated that quercetin showed the strongest binding affinity to AKT1 (- 9.7 kcal/mol). Furthermore, 100 ns MD simulation supported the stability and structural integrity of the quercetin-AKT1 complex over the entire simulation period. The findings of our investigation provide computational insights into the potential multi-target mechanisms of A. squamosa bioactive phytocompounds against RA, underscoring the necessity for further experimental validation and drug development. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00781-7.

papers.title: A Newly Curated Single Cell Sequencing Atlas Predicts Efferocytic-dependent Crosstalk in Hearts.
papers.authors: Meite I, Pesce L, Feinstein M, Thorp EB, Lantz CW.
papers.abstract: Cardiac repair after myocardial infarction (MI) requires coordinated immune cell communication, yet the signaling networks mediating this process and how they are disrupted in disease remain incompletely defined. MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on macrophages, promotes inflammation resolution, and its loss leads to inefficient cardiac repair. To investigate how MERTK shapes cardiac immune communication at single-cell resolution, we constructed a curated cardiac immune cell atlas integrating 36,932 cells/nuclei from 8 murine cardiac RNA sequencing datasets, yielding 22 annotated cell populations spanning myeloid, lymphoid, endothelial, and stromal compartments. We developed a cardiac-specific k-nearest neighbor classifier trained on this atlas that achieved an enhanced weighted F1 versus other widely used platforms. Applying our classifier to Mertk knockout (KO) versus control adult mice at 7 days post-MI revealed striking compositional differences including B cell expansion, reduction of CCR2+ macrophages, and enrichment of MHCII macrophages. The data are consistent with a shift from monocyte-derived macrophage-coordinated activation versus sustained adaptive immune activation. CellChat analysis revealed a reduction in total predicted interactions in KOs alongside near-doubling of per-interaction signaling strength. ARG1+ macrophages selectively lost SPP1 autocrine self-renewal signatures in KOs while preserving outgoing stromal signals. Moreover, a multi-sender Cyclophilin A-CD147 program deployed by mature macrophages across the stromal compartment was reprogrammed in KOs so that MHCII macrophages replaced mature macrophage subtypes as the predicted sender. These findings implicate MERTK in shaping macrophage identity and influencing the predicted intercellular communication architecture of the post-MI heart.
papers.venue: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology

papers.title: Evolution-Informed Viroinformatics Identifies Conserved Immune Targets with Predicted Lower Mutational Vulnerability Across Betacoronaviruses.
papers.authors: Alshammari J, Alqahtani HA, Alonaizan R, Rahman IU, Alzhrani K, Al-Hoshani N, Alwaili MA, Aziz T.
papers.abstract: The extensive evolutionary diversity and continuous mutational adaptation of betacoronaviruses represent a major challenge to the development of broadly protective countermeasures. This study applied an evolution-informed Viroinformatics framework to systematically identify conserved and immune targets with predicted lower mutational vulnerability across betacoronaviruses. The workflow integrated comparative sequence conservation and phylogenetic analysis with immunoinformatics-based epitope screening, HLA population coverage, mutational escape profiling, structural modeling, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. Conserved cytotoxic T-lymphocyte and helper T-lymphocyte epitopes were prioritized based on immunogenicity, antigenicity, safety, HLA binding potential, evolutionary conservation, and predicted resistance to mutational escape. Combined MHC class I and II analysis predicted a theoretical global population coverage of 99.92%, which requires experimental validation. The resulting 409-amino-acid multiepitope construct was predicted to be antigenic, non-allergenic, and physiochemically stable. Structural validation showed that 99.7% of the residues were located within favored or additionally allowed regions. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable interaction of the vaccine construct with TLR7, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation supported persistence of the predicted vaccine-receptor association. Overall, these findings provide a computational framework for prioritizing evolutionarily conserved immune targets and developing pre-emptive candidate epitopes showing predicted cross-betacoronavirus conservation within the analyzed dataset. Experimental studies evaluating HLA binding, cellular and humoral immunogenicity, recombinant expression, cross-reactivity, and in vivo protection are required to validate the predicted immunological potential and determine whether the proposed construct can provide broad protection against diverse betacoronaviruses.

papers.title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Distinct Pathogenic Subtypes in Hepatocyte- and Cholangiocyte-Directed Autoimmune Liver Injury.
papers.authors: Zhao P, Zhao L, Zhang H, Pu X, Qian J, Zhao Y, You Z, Ma X.
papers.abstract: Autoimmune liver diseases (AILDs) involve a group of distinct disorders, but the differences in pathogenic subpopulations that drive hepatocyte or bile duct injury remain unclear. This study characterizes immune niche heterogeneity across AILD subtypes using single-cell RNA sequencing and verifies findings with animal models. We identified distinct immune cell states and functions by analyzing the heterogeneity of T cell and macrophage subsets and the impact of non-immune cell-derived signals on macrophage identity. This allowed us to characterize two distinct immunopathogenic ecotypes between hepatitis and cholestatic phenotypes. Mechanistic analysis predicted the Bmp-Acvrl1/Eng-Fosb signaling axis as a critical transcriptional regulator driving the repair phenotype of macrophages. Notably, Eng (endoglin) emerged as a regulatory receptor controlling macrophage phenotypic transition, especially during the recovery phase of cholestatic disease. Collectively, this study provides a comprehensive atlas of immune cell niches across AILDs, offering new mechanistic insights into disease heterogeneity and identifying macrophage maturation as a promising target for stratified therapeutic intervention in cholestatic disease.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Network Analysis Identifies Diagnostic and Immune-Associated Hub Genes in Urothelial Carcinoma.
papers.authors: Alkhatib SN, Binsaleh AY, Al-Hoshani N, Bakhsh T, Alqahtani HA, Aziz T.
papers.abstract: Background: Urothelial carcinoma exhibits molecular heterogeneity, high recurrence, and progression rates, and is poorly diagnosed and treated. Transcriptomic and systems-biology analyses can detect dysregulated genes, signaling pathways, and interactions of immune cells. Proposed biomarkers, however, have not been validated, evaluated, and confirmed to be cell-type specific, limiting their potential for clinical translation. Methods: The transcriptomic data in GSE13507 were used to identify features of differential expression, functional enrichment, protein interaction network, and hub genes. Findings were assessed by using external validation, ROC and machine learning models, immune-infiltration analysis, single-cell expression profiling, and survival analysis. Results: In total, 7459 differentially expressed probes were detected, and pathways involved in immunity and cytokines were noted to be enriched. The best diagnostic performance was observed with IL6ST (AUC 0.927), LIFR (AUC 0.921), and JAK1 (AUC 0.843). We found a correlation between hub genes and infiltration of immune cells, and a difference in single-cell distribution; however, none of them was shown to have a significant association with overall survival. Conclusions: The IL-6/JAK/STAT hub gene network was highly diagnostic and immune-relevant in urothelial carcinoma and had limited prognostic significance. The three most promising candidates were IL6ST, LIFR, and JAK1. The genes identified in this study could be validated in tumor-normal pairs and in prospective clinical samples of future studies, accompanied by protein levels and functional studies.

papers.title: Peptidomics and Computational Docking Prioritize Candidate Peptide-Protein Associations Relevant to Upper-Gastrointestinal Biology in a Fermented Soy-Derived Postbiotic.
papers.authors: Tremblay A, Harms C, Nankar A, Gupta R, Buko A, Tompkins TA.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives : Gastro-AD ® (GAD) is a fermented soy-derived postbiotic supported by clinical and preclinical evidence related to gastric comfort and mucosal injury. Although fermentation-derived metabolites have been characterized, the peptide fraction remains poorly defined. This study characterized GAD peptides and explored their potential biological contexts. Methods : Untargeted peptidomics was used to identify soy-derived peptides in GAD and map them to source proteins. A diversity-sampling panel of ten peptides was selected using sequence, physicochemical, and predicted structural features. These peptides were screened against a human protein-structure library by computational docking, followed by GO enrichment and context-based prioritization of candidate interactors. Results: A total of 219 peptides, originating predominantly from soybean storage proteins, were identified. The GAD peptide fraction contained extensive overlapping sequence families and truncation ladders, consistent with extensive proteolytic processing. Three literature-reported antioxidant peptide sequences were identified as exact contiguous regions within longer GAD peptides. Large-scale docking against the screened human protein-structure library combined with GO-enrichment recurrence analysis and an independent review of top-ranked docking-derived candidates identified 180 candidate protein targets spanning innate immune and inflammatory defense, protease activity and peptide processing, extracellular-matrix remodeling, tissue repair and wound healing, and apoptotic signaling and epithelial turnover. Repeated randomized-affinity controls yielded substantially fewer FDR-significant GO terms than the observed docking-derived rankings, supporting non-random functional structure in the docking-derived protein rankings without establishing the accuracy of individual peptide-protein interactions. Context-based prioritization identified 43 unique Tier 1 and Tier 2 candidates with direct or context-dependent extracellular accessibility. The prioritized biological contexts included mucosal immune regulation, extracellular-matrix remodeling, epithelial turnover, and tissue restitution. Conclusions : The GAD peptide fraction described herein comprises multiple overlapping peptide families whose prioritized biological contexts center on mucosal defense, remodeling, and tissue restitution. These findings support further investigation of peptides as potential contributors to the multi-component biological properties of GAD.

papers.title: StainAI-Web: An Interactive Platform for Whole-Slide Microglial Morphology Analysis
papers.authors: Liu, D.-Y.; Chuang, H.-J.; Hsu, C.-H.; Chang, B.-M.; Ette, E.; Shih, M.; Liao, Y.-A.; Zehra, H.; Ali, S.; Tu, T.-R.; Lin, S.; Wang, P. C.; Shoykhet, M.; Tu, T.-W.
papers.abstract: Microglial morphology analysis has emerged as a critical approach in neuroinflammation research. The increasing availability of high-resolution and whole-slide histology images has created strong demand for robust, scalable analytical methods capable of efficiently processing these datasets. Existing approaches may require code-based local computation or prolonged processing times for whole-slide images, while manual morphology quantification remains labor-intensive. To address these limitations, we introduce StainAI-Web, a server that performs rapid, automated microglial morphology detection across whole-slide immunohistochemistry images in the cloud. The system provides interactive grayscale preprocessing and supports ROI-based regional quantification, allowing users to define specific tissue regions and systematically compare microglial populations across regions. An interactive visualization module dynamically updates quantitative summaries of morphological distributions as ROIs are selected or modified. Analysis results, including structured JSON files and morphology-annotated overlays, are downloadable for downstream analysis or integration into external computational pipelines. These integrated features provide an accessible framework for efficient and reproducible whole-slide microglial morphology analysis. The StainAI-Web is available at https://stainaiviewer.azurewebsites.net/.

papers.title: Human Organoids in Infectious Disease Research: From Host-Pathogen Interactions to Vaccine Development.
papers.authors: Zielinska D, Fol M, Druszczynska M.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Human organoids have emerged as physiologically relevant models bridging conventional two-dimensional cultures and animal models. This review summarizes advances in their application to infectious disease modeling and vaccine research, with emphasis on host-pathogen interactions, immune responses, and translational potential. Methods : A narrative review was conducted using targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and ScienceDirect. Publications from January 2000 to June 2026 were considered, and relevant evidence was qualitatively synthesized according to established applications, proof-of-concept studies, and prospective uses. Results: Human organoids have advanced the study of viral, bacterial, parasitic, and fungal infections by enabling investigation of pathogen entry, tissue tropism, barrier integrity, and immune responses in human-relevant systems. Immune and tonsil-derived organoids have also demonstrated applications in evaluating vaccine-induced immunity, comparing vaccine formulations, investigating mechanisms of immunogenicity, and identifying potential correlates of protection. Integration with single-cell and spatial omics, advanced imaging, and computational approaches is further expanding their utility. However, incomplete immune and vascular complexity, inter-model variability, limited standardization, scalability constraints, and insufficient validation against in vivo and clinical outcomes remain important challenges. Conclusions: Human organoids represent complementary human-relevant platforms with substantial potential for mechanistic and translational vaccinology. Further standardization and prospective validation are required to establish their predictive value for vaccine development.

papers.title: Addressing complex autofluorescence signatures in solid tissue samples to enhance full spectrum flow cytometry of non-immune cells.
papers.authors: Gkantsinikoudi C, Terranova-Barberio M, Dufton N.
papers.abstract: FSFC is an emerging technology that can greatly enhance our understanding of the single-cell proteomic landscape. We demonstrate that this application is applicable to cells derived from solid tissues which have traditionally been hampered by their complex autofluorescence signatures and lack of optimized tools for non-immune cells. We present a protocol and discuss key controls that minimize the impact of unmixing errors, enabling us to resolve multiple EC subpopulations isolated from different tissues in models of chronic tissue injury. Research topics vascular biology, cell heterogeneity, full spectrum flow cytometry.

papers.title: Interferon-Associated Inflammatory Remodeling and Oxidative Metabolic Repression Define the Skeletal Muscle Transcriptomic Landscape of δ-Sarcoglycan Deficiency.
papers.authors: Cancino-Bello A, Hernández-Somilleda M, Bahena-Culhuac E, García-González EG, Hernández-Hernández O, Coral-Vázquez RM, Hernández-Hernández JM.
papers.abstract: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R6, formerly LGMD2F, is caused by mutations in the δ-sarcoglycan ( Sgcd ) gene and is characterized by progressive skeletal muscle degeneration. Although loss of δ-SG protein compromises sarcolemma stability, how δ-sarcoglycan deficiency reshapes inflammatory and metabolic gene programs across distinct skeletal muscles remains incompletely defined. Here, we profiled soleus and extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles from wild-type and Sgcd -/- mice treated with vehicle or (-)-epicatechin, a dietary flavanol with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, using bulk RNA sequencing, pathway analysis, immune-cell deconvolution, and RT-qPCR validation. δ-sarcoglycan deficiency produced broad transcriptional remodeling while preserving baseline muscle-type identity. Across soleus and EDL, the dystrophic transcriptome was marked by interferon-associated inflammatory remodeling together with repression of oxidative and mitochondrial metabolic programs. Within this shared disease state, soleus displayed a stronger induced inflammatory component, including innate-sensing and macrophage-linked features. Computational deconvolution, which estimates immune-cell proportions from bulk transcriptomes (quanTIseq and mMCP-counter), supported genotype-dependent shifts in immune-cell signatures, with concordant monocyte/macrophage signals. Finally, (-)-epicatechin produced context-dependent transcriptional effects and attenuated a defined interferon/innate-sensing module in dystrophic soleus, as supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR. Together, these findings establish inflammatory remodeling with a prominent interferon component and oxidative metabolic repression as central transcriptional features of δ-sarcoglycan-deficient skeletal muscle, while revealing an amplified innate-sensing and immune-enriched module in dystrophic soleus that remains transcriptionally responsive to (-)-epicatechin treatment.

papers.title: Fenvalerate Induces Airway Epithelial Injury Through CHRM3-Associated NF-κB Activation.
papers.authors: Yang Y, Li J, Liu T, Sheng M, Liu J, Yang Z, Chu H, Jia A, Xu W.
papers.abstract: Fenvalerate (FEN) is a widely used pyrethroid insecticide with potential respiratory toxicity; however, its contribution to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-related pathological processes remains unclear. We investigated molecular mechanisms linking FEN exposure to airway epithelial injury. COPD transcriptomic datasets were integrated with predicted FEN targets, and candidate genes were prioritized using machine-learning algorithms. Immune infiltration and single-cell transcriptomic analyses were used to examine immune associations and cell-type-specific expression. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations assessed potential FEN-target interactions, followed by validation in BEAS-2B human bronchial epithelial cells. Intersecting FEN-COPD genes were enriched in inflammatory, immune-regulatory, neuroactive ligand-receptor, and epithelial injury-related pathways. Eight candidate genes showed distinct expression patterns across airway epithelial and immune cell populations. Computational analyses supported a potentially stable FEN-CHRM3 interaction. In BEAS-2B cells, FEN reduced viability, increased IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, promoted apoptosis, upregulated CHRM3, and enhanced IκBα and p65 phosphorylation. Pharmacological inhibition of CHRM3 or NF-κB partially attenuated these responses. Thus, FEN-induced epithelial inflammation and apoptosis may involve CHRM3-associated NF-κB activation, providing mechanistic insight into pesticide-related respiratory toxicity.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Shared Macrophage-Associated Inflammatory Signatures in MASLD/NAFLD and Rheumatoid Arthritis.
papers.authors: Yu W, Nie Q, Wu Y, Lan X, Liu J, Xu D, Guan S.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease/nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) may share inflammatory mechanisms, although their common cellular basis remains unclear. We integrated bulk transcriptomic datasets (GSE66676 and GSE55235), single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from murine RA synovium (GSE192504) and NASH liver (GSE129516), disease-association analysis, molecular docking, and in vitro experiments in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages. Bulk transcriptomic analysis identified 630 shared differentially expressed genes, including 344 concordantly upregulated genes enriched in immune response, cytokine and chemokine signaling, phagosome, Toll-like receptor signaling, and Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis; a strict dual-dataset intersection further defined 18 core genes significantly upregulated in both diseases. Immune-signature analysis indicated altered myeloid cell-associated inflammatory activity in both diseases, and several shared genes, including S100A8, S100A9, FCER1G, FCGR3A, LYZ, and MS4A7, correlated positively with monocyte/macrophage-related signatures. Single-cell analysis identified macrophage subsets with high S100a9 expression and elevated shared myeloid inflammatory signature scores in both RA synovium and NASH liver. Triptolide showed favorable predicted binding to the S100A8/A9 complex and reduced LPS-induced inflammatory cytokine secretion and expression of the six-gene signature in RAW264.7 cells, supporting the hypothesis that S100A9-associated inflammatory macrophage activation represents a candidate target for further investigation. These findings support a shared S100A9-positive inflammatory macrophage-associated program in MASLD/NAFLD and RA, and support the hypothesis that the S100A8/A9 complex represents a candidate target for further investigation.

papers.title: Identification of Transcriptional Signatures Associated with COPD in Immune and Epithelial-Stromal Cells Using Machine Learning Methods.
papers.authors: Ren J, Fan J, Bao Y, Guo W, Feng K, Hu J, Zhou W, Wang D, Lu L, Huang T, Cai YD.
papers.abstract: In the context of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), understanding gene expression patterns across various cell types is pivotal for disease comprehension, therapeutic development, and enhancement of patient prognosis. Nevertheless, the intricate interplay between immune and structural cells, along with their significance in COPD pathogenesis, remains only partially understood. This research employed multiple machine learning techniques to pinpoint marker genes exhibiting pronounced alterations between COPD patients and healthy individuals. We utilized six feature selection algorithms (LASSO, LightGBM, MCFS, RF, CATboost, and XGBoost) and three classification methods (DT, KNN, and RF) to analyze single-cell patient data. Cells were bifurcated into two subsets: immune cells and epithelial-stromal cells. Each cell, encompassing 21,237 genes, was labeled either as a healthy control or COPD.
