We identified a number of promising genes, such as FKBP5, which encodes a protein crucial for stress response regulation, and SCGB3A1, which is predominantly expressed in the respiratory tract and critical for regulating lung function. Both genes exhibit strong correlations with COPD. The study also underscored the potential roles of HLA-DRB1 and HSP90AA1 in COPD pathogenesis. Our findings underscore the unparalleled potential of machine learning in identifying genetic markers for intricate diseases like COPD, paving the way for targeted therapeutic advancements.

papers.title: Follistatin-like Protein 1 Contributes to Acute Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury by Enhancing Neuroinflammation Through the Modulation of Interferon Regulatory Factor 5-Mediated Macrophage Activation.
papers.authors: Luo Y, Ni S, Peng L, Zhu L, Chen T, Wang P, Li Z.
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose : Follistatin-like protein 1 (Fstl1) is a secreted glycoprotein with context-dependent inflammatory activity. We investigated whether Fstl1 is a reproducible feature of traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) and whether it regulates macrophage activation through interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5). Methods : A target-blind analysis integrated four public SCI bulk transcriptomic cohorts with single-cell and spatial datasets. Findings were tested in wild-type and Fstl1+/- mice after SCI using spinal cord RNA sequencing, molecular and histological assays, behavioral testing, and bone marrow-derived macrophages with IRF5 gain- and loss-of-function. Adult-induced Postn-CreER-mediated Fstl1 deletion was evaluated in fibroblast-macrophage non-contact co-cultures. Results : The public-data screen reduced 440 cross-cohort candidates to four non-structural extracellular genes, including Fstl1. Fstl1 was consistently upregulated across SCI cohorts, correlated with myeloid signatures, and was predominantly associated with non-myeloid cell sources in single-cell data. Experimental SCI increased spinal Fstl1 and inflammatory cytokines, whereas partial Fstl1 depletion reduced tissue damage and improved locomotor recovery. Fibroblast Fstl1 deletion reduced macrophage iNOS, Il6, and Tnf and increased Arg-1 and Il10 in co-culture. Spinal cord RNA sequencing showed broad remodeling of immune and tissue-related programs after Fstl1 depletion. Computational perturbation and experimental validation identified IRF5 as a downstream mediator. Recombinant Fstl1 increased IRF5, iNOS, and CD80 while reducing Arg-1 and CD163; IRF5 silencing reversed these changes. Conclusions : Fstl1 is a reproducible SCI-associated extracellular candidate that supports IRF5-dependent inflammatory macrophage activation. Targeting the Fstl1-IRF5 axis may help limit secondary neuroinflammation after SCI.

papers.title: Metabolic Dysfunction and T-Cell Exhaustion in Colorectal Cancer: Mechanisms, Microenvironment Remodeling, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.authors: Jeon J, Baek HS, Park K, Park MN, Heo NH, Cheon S, Kim G, Kim S.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. Metabolic disorders such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome are associated with CRC risk. Metabolic abnormalities may contribute to colorectal tumorigenesis and reshape the tumor immune microenvironment, which in turn influence immune dysfunction and therapeutic resistance. Exhausted CD8 + T cells exhibit impaired effector function, sustained inhibitory receptor expression, and transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. Metabolic stressors within the CRC microenvironment may modulate T-cell function and exhaustion-associated states. Additionally, other immune populations (natural killer cells, macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells) may develop distinct dysfunctional or immunosuppressive states. Recent single-cell and spatial studies have indicated the heterogeneity of these immunometabolic interactions in CRC. This review examines the interactions of the systemic and tumor-associated metabolic alterations with T-cell exhaustion and other forms of immune dysfunction in CRC. We discuss the influence of glucose, lipid, amino acid, and mitochondrial metabolism, hypoxia, microbiota-derived metabolites, and chronic inflammation in shaping tumor-immune interactions. Finally, we reviewed therapeutic strategies targeting immunometabolic pathways and their potential integration with immune checkpoint blockade. Overall, understanding these interactions may help identify immunometabolic vulnerabilities for informing precise therapeutic strategies for CRC.

papers.title: Tissue Factor Expression Is Associated with Distinct Pattern of Immune-Cell Infiltration in the Ovarian Tumor Microenvironment.
papers.authors: Mohiuddin TM, Binte Hafiz F, Sheng W, Zhang C, Al-Rawe M, Zeppernick F, Tchaikovski S, Meinhold-Heerlein I, Hussain AF.
papers.abstract: Tissue factor (TF) has been implicated in tumor progression and immune regulation, but its cellular sources and relationship with immune infiltration in ovarian cancer remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (GSE232314), analyses of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) ovarian cancer cohort, and multiplex immunofluorescence in an independent 25-case tissue microarray (TMA). Single-cell analysis showed that TF expression was concentrated in tumor epithelial cells and a discrete endothelial subpopulation, with minimal expression in immune and other stromal compartments. In the TCGA cohort, TF expression was not significantly associated with tumor stage, grade, disease-free survival, or overall survival. In TF-stratified analyses, however, high CD8 + T cell infiltration was associated with improved survival in the low-TF expression subgroup (HR = 0.60) but with worse survival in the high-TF subgroup (HR = 1.72); high M1 macrophage infiltration was associated with improved survival only in the low-TF subgroup. TF expression correlated negatively with estimated CD8 + T cell, memory B cell, and M1 macrophage infiltration and positively with naïve B cell infiltration. In the TMA cohort, high-TF tumors showed significantly lower CD56 + NK-cell and CD68 + macrophage infiltration and a lower CD68/CD163 ratio. Together, these findings show cross-sectional associations between TF expression and reduced measured abundance of several antitumor immune populations and a stratum-dependent association between CD8 + T cell infiltration and survival. These associations were not fully concordant between the transcriptomic (TCGA) and protein-level (TMA) cohorts and require prospective, formally tested validation. TF warrants further investigation as a candidate immune-context biomarker in ovarian cancer.

papers.title: Podocyte Biology in Pediatric Glomerular Disease: From Slit Diaphragm Assembly to Genotype-Guided Therapy-A Narrative Review.
papers.authors: Todorović P, Kopilaš A, Racetin A, Maglica M, Rizikalo A, Raguž F, Kelam N, Vukojević K.
papers.abstract: The podocyte is a terminally differentiated cell whose foot processes and slit diaphragm form the final layer of the glomerular filtration barrier. Because podocytes are not effectively replaced after birth, and nephron number is fixed before it, their cumulative loss converts congenital and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and Alport syndrome into a shared trajectory towards chronic kidney disease. This narrative review, based on a structured search of three databases with the cited evidence classified as pediatric, adult, mixed or preclinical, connects podocyte biology with pediatric nephrology. We follow maturation and the modules whose disruption produces disease, a genetic architecture in which diagnostic yield falls steeply with age at onset, and the convergence of genetic, mechanical, metabolic and immune insults on podocyte depletion. Single-cell and spatial atlases, organoids, glomerulus-on-a-chip systems and human tissue are compared as partly discordant platforms. A molecular result currently changes a small, defined set of clinical decisions. No podocyte-derived urinary marker has been shown in children to add information beyond proteinuria and filtration rate, anti-nephrin antibody assays are not yet standardized, and kidney biopsy remains the reference standard. We set out an integrated diagnostic pathway, state the limitations of the evidence and define research priorities.

papers.title: AI-Guided Histopathological and Molecular Phenotyping of Salivary Glands in Sjögren's Disease: Subtyping, Mechanistic Insights, and Translational Implications-A Systematic Review and Structured Functional Synthesis.
papers.authors: Ardila CM, Pineda-Vélez E, Vivares-Builes AM.
papers.abstract: Background/objectives Salivary-gland biopsy is central to Sjögren's disease (SjD) assessment, but conventional measures incompletely capture glandular heterogeneity. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) applications to SjD salivary-gland histopathology and molecular profiling, including biological and translational validation. Methods PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched. Eligible studies used salivary-gland tissue as the primary analytical substrate or provided substantive glandular validation of systemic AI/ML findings. Evidence was synthesized functionally because of methodological heterogeneity. Results Twenty-five studies were included. AI/ML identified histopathological and molecular phenotypes spanning immune/interferon activation, tissue architecture and immune-cell organization, epithelial stress and metabolic/cell-death remodeling, and translational response. Only a limited subset progressed beyond computational or tissue-level confirmation to functional perturbation, pharmacological testing, in vivo validation, or human treatment-response assessment. Recurrent public-dataset reuse, small cohorts, heterogeneous pipelines, and limited independent validation constrained reproducibility. Conclusions AI/ML supports multidimensional SjD glandular phenotyping and shows emerging translational potential, but demonstrated clinical or therapeutic utility remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter validation is required before AI-derived glandular phenotypes can inform routine patient stratification or therapeutic decision-making.

papers.title: Multi-Frame Reconstruction via Clutter Filtering for Computational Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Microflow Imaging.
papers.authors: Liang D, Chen D, Qian X, Zhong Y, Xia Y, Zhang J.
papers.abstract: Objective Existing computational reconstruction methods for plane-wave ultrasound imaging (PWI) often neglect the interference of strong tissue signals with weak flow-related scattering signals in microflow imaging. This study aims to develop a multi-frame computational ultrasound reconstruction technique that integrates multi-frame sparse constraints with RF signal preprocessing strategies to facilitate the suppression of tissue signals and background noise. Methods We propose multi-frame reconstruction of contrast-enhanced ultrasound microflow imaging. First, to prevent tissue signals from diluting the sparsity of multi-frame data, we apply singular value decomposition directly to the raw radio-frequency data, attenuating tissue-dominated components before beamforming. This yields sparser data and increases the relative contribution of flow-related components in the optimization. Results The method was evaluated in contrast-enhanced microflow simulations and an exploratory in vivo experiment involving one rabbit. Under the tested conditions, VrUSi reduced background signals and produced narrower apparent intensity profiles than delay-and-sum and single-frame computational reconstruction. In the single-rabbit experiment, VrUSi yielded higher image-domain BCR values and smaller apparent-profile FWHM values across the analyzed temporal windows. These metrics are interpreted as background suppression and apparent profile compactness under the tested conditions, rather than as evidence of improved physical contrast or spatial resolution. The findings support feasibility only for visualizing flow-related structures in the tested rabbit lower-limb acquisition.

papers.title: Integrative Multi-Database Bioinformatics Characterization of FANCE in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Prognostic, Epigenetic, Immune, and ncRNA Associations.
papers.authors: Kim YC, Lee KS, Kim HR, Kim J.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: The Fanconi anemia complementation group E (FANCE) is a protein component of the Fanconi anemia (FA) DNA repair complex and contributes to genome integrity. However, its molecular and clinical relevance in liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) remains incompletely understood. This study characterized the FANCE expression, prognosis, epigenetics, immune responses, noncoding RNA (ncRNA) networks, and other related molecular processes in LIHC. Materials and Methods: An integrative multi-database bioinformatics analysis was conducted using public databases and web-based platforms. FANCE expression, DNA methylation, co-expression profiles, and functional enrichment; immune cell infiltration; miRNA-ncRNA, chemical-gene, and protein-protein interactions; treatment response; and survival were evaluated. Results: FANCE expression was higher in LIHC than in non-tumor liver tissues, and this was linked to shorter survival duration. Promoter methylation was lower in LIHC, and select CpG sites were related to FANCE expression and survival. Immune analyses identified heterogeneous relationships between FANCE and inferred immune cell populations. hsa-miR-101-3p was reduced in LIHC, negatively correlated with FANCE, and linked to prolonged survival; subsequent network analysis identified candidate lncRNAs, small ncRNAs, circRNA-linked genes, and pseudogenes. FANCE-related transcriptional profiles were enriched in the cell cycle, DNA replication, FA, and other DNA-repair processes, whereas negatively correlated genes were mainly linked to hepatic metabolic functions. Exploratory treatments identified drug-dependent survival patterns related to FANCE expression and elevated levels in responders to specific immune-checkpoint inhibitors, although the discriminatory performance was modest. Conclusions: Increased FANCE expression in LIHC was linked to molecular features involving DNA methylation, immune cell composition, ncRNA-related interactions, and DNA repair programs as well as shorter survival. These findings provide an integrated molecular context for FANCE in LIHC but do not establish a causal regulation or therapeutic predictive value. Independent clinical and experimental validation studies are warranted to determine its biological and clinical significance.

papers.title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery.
papers.authors: Carata E, Mariano S, Tenuzzo BA, Panzarini E.
papers.abstract: Background : Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives : This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods : A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results : Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions : Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.

papers.title: NET-Associated Transcriptional Signatures and T-Cell Functional States During Allogeneic CAR-γδT-Cell Therapy: A Longitudinal Single-Cell Analysis.
papers.authors: Yao L, Liu Z, Wang Y, Gu W, Bai YF.
papers.abstract: Background CAR T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, although conventional autologous αβ CAR-T products remain limited by complex manufacturing, variable persistence, and relapse risk. γδT cells provide a promising donor source for next-generation off-the-shelf CAR-T therapies due to their MHC-independent tumor recognition, potent cytotoxicity, and minimal risk of graft-versus-host disease; however, the determinants of treatment durability following allogeneic CAR-γδT-cell therapy remain poorly defined. NETs have recently emerged as key immunoregulatory components of the TME, where excessive NET formation sustains inflammation, reshapes immune-stromal interactions, and impairs lymphocyte function, yet their impact on CAR-T-cell fate is largely unknown. Methods In this study, we performed longitudinal single-cell transcriptomic profiling of patients treated with allogeneic CAR-γδT cells and integrated ligand-receptor inference, pathway enrichment, and transcriptional regulatory analyses. Results We identified a 69-gene NET-associated transcriptional signature in the neutrophil population captured in PBMC samples. The NET-associated transcriptional score increased longitudinally in the single patient who subsequently relapsed, whereas longitudinal patterns varied across individual patients. Exploratory analyses identified associations between NET-associated transcriptional activity and T-cell functional programs, including an inverse association with proliferation. NicheNet, pathway enrichment, and SCENIC analyses highlighted candidate inflammatory and regulatory programs involving IL-1-related signaling, adhesion pathways, SMAD3 regulon activity, and E2F-related proliferative programs. Analysis of an independent cohort provided supportive evidence for related inflammatory transcriptional patterns, although differences in therapeutic platform and cellular composition limited direct validation. Discussion Together, these findings suggest that NET-associated inflammatory states may be linked to peripheral immune remodeling and altered circulating T-cell functional states during CAR-γδT-cell therapy. Larger longitudinal cohorts, more comprehensive clinical annotation, and orthogonal measurements of NET formation are needed to establish the clinical and mechanistic significance of these associations.

papers.title: Dietary Curcumin Protects Common Carp ( Cyprinus carpio ) Against Potassium Permanganate-Induced Toxicity: Hematological, Immunological, Oxidative, and Molecular Docking Evidence.
papers.authors: Eroğlu M, Mişe Yonar S, Tanrıkulu D, Uslu H, Yonar ME.
papers.abstract: Potassium permanganate treatment can adversely affect fish physiology despite its usefulness in aquaculture. This study evaluated the protective effects of dietary curcumin against potassium permanganate-induced disturbances in common carp (Cyprinus carpio). Fish were fed a basal diet or diets supplemented with 1%, 2%, or 4% curcumin for eight weeks, with or without subsequent exposure to potassium permanganate at 2 mg/L for 30 min daily for seven days. Hematological and immune parameters and oxidative status in the liver, kidney, spleen, and gill were assessed. Potassium permanganate exposure altered blood and immune parameters, increased lipid peroxidation, and weakened antioxidant defenses. Curcumin supplementation alleviated these effects, with protection evident at 1%, the lowest dietary inclusion level tested, and further improvements in selected parameters at 4%. Inclusion levels below 1% were not evaluated, so the minimum effective level remains unknown. Molecular docking predicted interactions between curcumin and the antioxidant enzymes SOD, CAT, GPx, and GST at structurally plausible binding sites. These computational findings were interpreted alongside the biological results as supportive, hypothesis-generating evidence rather than confirmation of functional effects on these enzymes in vivo. Overall, dietary curcumin showed potential to reduce the physiological disturbances associated with repeated potassium permanganate exposure. Further dose-response studies should evaluate inclusion levels below 1% to identify effective and economically viable supplementation rates and determine whether curcumin affects the antiparasitic or antibacterial efficacy of potassium permanganate.

papers.title: Unveiling a dual-pathway prognostic model: Integrating T cell-related and ubiquitination-related genes in lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Zeng S, Gao H, Liang H, Zhang D.
papers.abstract: The prognosis of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is closely associated with T-cell function and ubiquitination; however, the underlying mechanisms have remained elusive. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify robust prognostic biomarkers. Using The Cancer Genome Atlas (n=515) and the Gene Expression Omnibus Series GSE31210 (n=226) datasets, an integrated differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression were performed to identify a prognostic signature. Based on an eight-gene risk model, patients were stratified into high-risk and low-risk groups. The model was subsequently evaluated through immune infiltration analysis, drug sensitivity assessment and reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) validation. Although the RT-qPCR validation cohort was relatively small (n=20), limiting statistical power, the observed expression trends were consistent with the bioinformatics findings. An eight-gene signature comprising RNF180, MAP3K3, TRIM2, RNF125, RWDD3, RNF144B, KCTD5 and TRIM27 was identified. In the training cohort, the risk model achieved area under the curve values of >0.6 for 1-, 3- and 5-year survival and was successfully validated in the independent GSE31210 cohort. A nomogram incorporating the risk score and M stage showed potential clinical utility within a limited threshold probability range. The high-risk group exhibited distinct immune infiltration patterns and significantly higher Tumour Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion scores. Drug sensitivity analysis identified 125 agents, including axitinib, with significantly different half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) values between the two risk groups. Specifically, high-risk patients exhibited higher IC 50 values for certain drugs, indicating lower sensitivity, whereas low-risk patients were more likely to respond to these agents. RT-qPCR analysis of an expanded cohort of 20 paired LUAD and adjacent normal tissues confirmed the differential expression of five key genes: KCTD5, MAP3K3, RNF144B, TRIM2 and TRIM27 . In conclusion, this novel prognostic model integrating T cell-related and ubiquitination-related genes provides a potential tool for risk stratification and personalized treatment in LUAD. It may also help clinicians identify high-risk patients who could benefit from closer follow-up or targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Pulmonary Disease and NF-κB-Associated Responses in Mice Infected with Two Klebsiella pneumoniae Isolates.
papers.authors: Song R, Xu J, Pu D, Wang N, Syed MA, Zhao J, Cao B.
papers.abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKP) causes invasive disease, but pulmonary macrophage responses remain incompletely defined. We compared strain 55055, used as a classical K. pneumoniae (cKP) comparator, with strain 46274, operationally classified as hvKP, using a pneumonia model, single-cell RNA sequencing of pooled lungs, and RAW 264.7 macrophages. At the same inoculum, strain 46274 had higher lung burdens and greater mortality than strain 55055; representative sections showed more extensive inflammatory-cell infiltration, whereas no pairwise difference in animal-level H&E scores remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment. Because neither pulmonary burden nor disease stage was matched, immune-response differences cannot be separated from effects of unequal bacterial exposure or differences in disease progression. Descriptive pooled-library analysis showed differences in immune-cell composition and CellChat-inferred communication. In the single day-2 strain 46274 pooled library, SPP1 + macrophages comprised a larger fraction than in the corresponding strain 55055 pooled library and had high inflammatory-response, chemokine, and bacterial-recognition gene-set scores; this library-level observation was not independently validated in individual animals. Tissue-level staining showed numerical day-2 differences in CD86- and CD206-positive-cell abundance, but adjusted pairwise comparisons did not confirm strain-specific differences and the data do not demonstrate M1/M2 macrophage polarization. NF-κB-associated imaging findings remained qualitative. In vitro, strain 46274 showed lower adhesion to and phagocytosis by RAW 264.7 macrophages, but higher IL-6 and TNF-α readouts and stronger qualitative late p65 nuclear localization. These in vitro observations were obtained in RAW 264.7 cells within one experimental run and should not be extrapolated directly to primary pulmonary macrophages. Overall, in this strain-pair murine model, strain 46274 was associated with more severe pulmonary disease and NF-κB-associated inflammatory readouts.

papers.title: Multi-omics insights into immune dysregulation and candidate biological programs in kawasaki disease: toward precision immunomodulation.
papers.authors: Han Y, Liu J, Song C, Fu L, Gu Y, Zeng Y, Zou Z.
papers.abstract: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an immune-mediated pediatric vasculitis characterized by dynamic interactions among genetic susceptibility, innate and adaptive immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular remodeling. Although intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy substantially reduces coronary complications, 10%-20% of patients show persistent or recurrent fever after initial IVIG treatment, and reliable clinically validated molecular approaches for diagnosis, treatment-response prediction, and coronary-risk stratification remain unavailable. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, single-cell sequencing, proteomics, metabolomics, and microbiome profiling, have expanded our understanding of KD-associated immune dysregulation. However, the clinical interpretation of these molecular findings remains challenging because of limited cohort sizes, heterogeneous control populations, treatment-related confounding, and insufficient external validation. In this review, we integrate evidence across multiple molecular layers and propose a framework in which current KD multi-omics findings converge into candidate biological programs rather than fixed molecular subtypes. These programs may represent temporally dynamic biological states along a shared inflammatory trajectory, influenced by disease phase, cellular composition, genetic background, and treatment exposure. Synthesized from convergent multi-omics evidence rather than derived from formal molecular classification, these candidate biological programs include myeloid inflammatory activation characterized by S100A8/A9 and IL-1/NF- κ B signaling, interferon-associated immune responses, and vascular injury/remodeling responses involving endothelial activation and extracellular matrix regulation. Current evidence supports biologically meaningful molecular programs that may contribute to clinical heterogeneity, but prospective validation is required before molecular signatures can be applied as clinical classifiers or treatment-selection tools. Integrating multi-omics approaches with functional validation, longitudinal sampling, and multicenter studies may facilitate the development of precision immunomodulation strategies for Kawasaki disease.

papers.title: Spatial heterogeneity in glioblastoma: linking single-cell and spatial multi-omics to vaccine immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Yuan J, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most lethal primary brain tumor, with survival still limited despite advances in multimodal treatment. The tumor's profound heterogeneity--across patients, within individual tumors, and over time--has frustrated every class of therapeutic intervention. Recent developments in single-cell and spatial omics technologies have substantially advanced our understanding of this heterogeneity. No longer viewed as a uniform mass, GBM is now recognized as a spatially organized ecosystem of distinct malignant cell states, immune neighborhoods, and metabolic niches that interact across macroscopic distances. Spatial transcriptomics has revealed that malignant cells exist along a continuum of transcriptional programs--from neural progenitor-like to mesenchymal-like--that are not randomly distributed but organized into structured regions with a multi-layered architecture associated with hypoxia. Spatial proteomics and imaging mass cytometry have complemented these findings by mapping protein-level immune landscapes, uncovering cellular neighborhoods associated with survival and identifying spatially defined immunosuppressive niches. This review summarizes current knowledge from single-cell and spatial multi-omic studies of GBM, with an emphasis on the spatial organization of malignant cell states, the architecture of the tumor immune microenvironment, and the implications of these findings for therapeutic development, particularly vaccine immunotherapy. We argue that spatial technologies do not replace existing therapeutic pipelines but address a critical blind spot: the spatial dimension that bulk measurements cannot see.

papers.title: Integrative single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analysis identifies monocyte/macrophage senescence-associated candidate genes in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
papers.authors: Chen X, Wu W, Liu Y, Lian G, Liu Q.
papers.abstract: Background Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vascular disorder characterized by immune dysregulation and vascular remodeling. Cellular senescence modulates immune responses, but its role in PAH, particularly in monocytes/macrophages, remains unclear. Here, we integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data to identify senescence-associated candidate genes associated with monocytes/macrophages in PAH. Methods Publicly available single-cell RNA-seq data from PAH and control pulmonary vascular tissues were analyzed. A senescence-associated score was calculated for each cell based on MSigDB gene sets. Senescence-associated genes in monocytes/macrophages were identified through correlation and differential expression screening, and further examined in bulk transcriptomic datasets. Bulk transcriptomic discovery used GSE113439, GSE117261, and GSE254617. A sample-title audit identified 68 shared PHBI identifiers between GSE117261 and GSE254617; therefore, the merged data represented 257 expression profiles from 189 unique subjects. LASSO, Random Forest, and XGBoost were used as complementary feature-selection approaches, and genes jointly retained by the three algorithms were defined as candidates for evaluation in independent cohorts. Results Single-cell RNA-seq identified 14 cell types in PAH pulmonary vascular tissues, with dendritic cells, T cells, and monocytes/macrophages exhibiting the highest senescence-associated scores. Integrative screening identified 405 senescence-associated genes enriched in monocytes/macrophages. Multi-algorithm screening prioritized 10 candidate genes for subsequent evaluation. After within-cohort multiple-testing correction, external cohort analyses reproduced the discovery-stage expression directions for RGS1 , PHLDA1 , MAFB , and RNF13 in lung tissue cohorts, and for MAFB in a PBMC cohort. With nominal P values, RGS1 was significantly upregulated in GSE48149 and GSE53408 (both lung), and PHLDA1 was upregulated in GSE48149 (lung). MAFB was significantly downregulated in GSE33463 (PBMC) and GSE48149 (lung), whereas RNF13 was downregulated in GSE15197 and GSE48149 (both lung). Functional analysis revealed significant enrichment of immune-inflammatory and phagocytosis-related pathways among the candidate genes. Consensus clustering based on the candidate genes classified PAH patients into two exploratory transcriptomic groups with distinct expression and pathway activity profiles. In vivo evaluation in an MCT-induced PAH rat model showed seven significant direction-consistent changes, two direction-consistent nonsignificant trends, and one discordant gene ( PDE4B ), supporting tissue-level expression concordance. Conclusion These analyses identify a Mono.Macs-associated senescence-related candidate gene set in PAH. Independent expression analyses provide additional support for RGS1 , PHLDA1 , MAFB , and RNF13 as candidate genes for subsequent mechanistic and functional validation.

papers.title: Functional single-cell omics in gynecological cancers immunotherapy: from heterogeneity dissection to clinical translation.
papers.authors: Li DM, Pei KG, Yang BW, Qie MR, Xu JF, Zhong L, Song L.
papers.abstract: Ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancers represent major threats to women's health worldwide. The profound heterogeneity of their immune microenvironments has rendered immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, particularly PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, far less effective than anticipated in gynecological malignancies. Conventional research approaches, constrained by coarse analytical resolution, are insufficient to unravel the underlying mechanisms of this therapeutic shortfall. Functional single-cell omics technologies, including single-cell RNA sequencing, single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and multi-omics integration, have provided a new framework for systematically studying the tumor immune microenvironment across three progressive dimensions: cellular identity, functional state, and spatial localization. This review systematically synthesizes the applications of this technological toolkit in the three major gynecological cancers. It reveals distinct bottlenecks across the three dimensions. In ovarian cancer, the core obstacle lies in the spatial dimension, where cancer-associated fibroblast-mediated physical barriers and pro-angiogenic macrophage subsets together construct a "spatial exclusion" microenvironment. In cervical cancer, the principal bottleneck resides in the functional dimension, where HPV status and histological subtype drive a "functional disability" phenotype, in which T cells infiltrate but fail to achieve effective activation, with therapy resistance-associated immune evasion clones further exacerbating functional impairment. In endometrial cancer, however, the immune fate is governed by the identity dimension, where molecular subtypes dictate the baseline nature of immune infiltration, and autophagy-related cellular subpopulations may offer new insights into intratumoral heterogeneity. Although single-cell omics has identified immunologically actionable targets with translational potential, including TREM2 + macrophages and the LAG-3/TIM-3 dual-target axis, clinical translation remains constrained by technical and biological bottlenecks, including stringent requirements for tissue sample quality, high assay costs, lack of standardized analytical pipelines, and the discordance between transcriptomic profiles and protein-level functionality.

papers.title: Tumor antigens across cancer progression: from immune recognition and selection to precision cancer immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Leong SP.
papers.abstract: Tumor antigens provide the molecular interface between malignant transformation and host immunity, but their biological significance is determined by more than their molecular existence. Antigen clonality, abundance, processing, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) presentation, dendritic-cell function, T-cell recognition, spatial immune organization, and the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) collectively determine whether an antigen becomes immunologically visible and therapeutically actionable. Across cancer progression, tumor-cell antigenic states and the TME undergo reciprocal selection: immune pressure can eliminate highly visible clones while favoring antigen-loss variants, HLA defects, immune exclusion, suppressive myeloid and stromal states, and treatment-resistant populations. Recent single-cell, spatial and three-dimensional imaging, as well as immunopeptidomic studies show that this evolution is heterogeneous across tumor regions and anatomical compartments rather than a uniform linear process. This review therefore advances an antigen-TME co-evolution framework linking primary tumors, lymphatic and nodal immune compartments, systemic dissemination, distant metastatic niches, therapy, minimal residual disease, and recurrence. It critically evaluates the strengths and limitations of the classical immunoediting model; compares melanoma, breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, sarcoma, and virus-associated cancers according to antigen source, clonality, presentation competence, immune architecture, and dominant therapeutic bottleneck; and examines clinical translation through checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, vaccines, antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, immunopeptidomics, and computational antigen prediction. Particular attention is given to the gap between predicted peptide binding and verified presentation or immunogenicity, the need for longitudinal rather than single-biopsy profiling, and the requirement for prospective validation of artificial-intelligence models. The central conclusion is that tumor antigens become clinically meaningful only when antigenic state and microenvironmental context are assessed together, providing a more rigorous foundation for precision cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: Longitudinal peripheral immune dynamics during anti-programmed cell death 1 neoadjuvant therapy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
papers.authors: Li L, Meng L, Chen X, Li J, Li P, Dong B, Huang C, Zhou W, Li N, Sun G, Li J, Tan G, Jiang L, Tian D.
papers.abstract: Introduction Anti-programmed cell death 1 (PD-1)-based neoadjuvant therapy is increasingly used for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but paired peripheral immune dynamics and their exploratory relationship to response remain incompletely characterized. Methods We performed a retrospective longitudinal flow-cytometry study of 39 patients with ESCC treated with anti-PD-1-based neoadjuvant therapy, including 20 patients with paired pre-treatment and post-treatment/preoperative peripheral immune profiles. The primary paired analysis tested 75 marker-defined immune features using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Exploratory extensions included response-associated changes in candidate immune features, clinical burden context, baseline-dependence, and public tissue-context bioinformatics. Public tissue data were used only as descriptive tissue context. Results Four features reached FDR q + CD8 T cells, PD-1 + Vδ1 γδ T cells, PD-1 + Vδ2 γδ T cells, and CD19 + B cells. PD-1-defined features were interpreted as assay-defined detectable PD-1 staining readouts because therapeutic anti-PD-1 receptor occupancy or epitope masking may affect post-treatment staining. CD19 + B cells remained the non-PD-1 q + natural killer (NK) cells was the strongest nominal exploratory and hypothesis-generating signal. Discussion These data support treatment-associated marker-defined peripheral immune dynamics and generate response-linked hypotheses requiring prospective validation.

papers.title: Autophagy as a potential link between progesterone responsiveness and endometrial immune function in recurrent implantation failure.
papers.authors: Guo L, Xie J, Wang M, Ma S, Zhang X, Guan Y.
papers.abstract: Recurrent implantation failure (RIF) describes a clinical outcome rather than a single diagnosis or immune disorder. During progesterone-driven decidualization, changes in stromal metabolism and epithelial secretion accompany the production of signals that support uterine natural killer (uNK) cell residency. Autophagy contributes to these changes, although its role in RIF is unresolved. Genetic studies in mice and human stromal cells implicate autophagy-related proteins in progesterone responses and decidual differentiation. Some RIF tissue studies, however, report increased autophagy-associated signals. Increased flux accompanies impaired progesterone responses in some stromal models and improved decidualization in others. These contrasting findings may reflect the need to maintain autophagic activity within a suitable range for each cell compartment and cycle phase, rather than a uniform deficit. Progesterone-responsive stromal cells release interleukin 15 (IL-15) and related signals that recruit and program uNK cells. Their residency may also depend on epithelial secretion, adhesion, and matrix remodeling. In cycling human endometrium, activated uNK cells contribute to tissue quality control by clearing senescent maternal decidual cells; the embryo is not the target of this process. Single-cell and spatial studies of RIF endometrium have identified altered epithelial, stromal, and NK states. Whether progesterone resistance causes these cellular changes and, in turn, implantation failure remains unknown. This review examines the evidence for these relationships and the experiments needed to assess autophagic flux beyond static markers and uNK function beyond cell abundance. Current evidence does not support routine NK testing or autophagy-directed treatment in RIF.

papers.title: Spatial architecture shapes programmed cell death-associated immune niches and therapeutic resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
papers.authors: Yin Y, Wang J, Li D, Qiu D.
papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by VHL-HIF pathway alterations, lipid remodeling, abnormal angiogenesis, and marked immune heterogeneity. These features create a highly vascular yet unevenly perfused microenvironment in which vascular dysfunction, hypoxia, stromal barriers, and myeloid clearance influence whether cell death becomes immunologically productive. Although immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and HIF-2α inhibitors have improved outcomes, primary and acquired resistance and discordant responses among lesions remain common. Bulk PD-L1 expression, immune-cell abundance, and cell-death-related transcript signatures do not resolve this heterogeneity. Following current nomenclature, regulated cell death (RCD) is the mechanistically preferred umbrella term; we retain programmed cell death (PCD) in the conceptual label because it remains widely used in the RCC oncology literature, while requiring RCD execution-level evidence for mechanistic claims. Single-cell and spatial multi-omics studies increasingly show that the identity of the dying cell, execution of the death program, accessibility of death-derived material, and the recipient immune cells operate as a coupled local system. We define a PCD-associated immune niche as a spatial tissue state in which representative, non-exclusive immune-routing axes can direct tumor-cell death toward cDC1-mediated cross-presentation and adaptive antitumor immunity, TAM-dominant efferocytosis and tissue repair, or intermediate mixed states. This Review focuses predominantly on ccRCC, evaluates ferroptosis, apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, and PANoptosis, and briefly considers emerging RCD modalities for which ccRCC evidence is less mature. We further propose composite spatial biomarkers and mechanism-guided combinations that link cellular source, execution evidence, immune routing, and clinical outcome.

papers.title: Host-Microbe Crosstalk in Sjögren's Disease: Epithelial Type I Interferon Amplification, Loss of Short-Chain Fatty Acid Restraint, and the Effector-Phase Focus of Validated Therapy.
papers.authors: Yu M, Jo D, Hwang Y, Han K.
papers.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands, long framed as a lymphocyte-driven disorder in which immune cells destroy the target tissue. Genomic, epigenetic, microbiome, and single-cell and spatial studies have since shown the glandular epithelium and the microbial environment to be active participants rather than passive bystanders. This review asks whether host susceptibility and microbiome change can be joined into one continuous axis, following it from genetic and epigenetic susceptibility, through microbiome change read functionally rather than taxonomically, to the crosstalk that converts microbial signals into a host response and the cell states carrying it in human tissue. Two axes run through the whole sequence: the type I interferon (IFN) response and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolism. Read against them, every disease-modifying therapy with validated efficacy so far acts in the downstream B-cell effector axis, whereas the upstream IFN axis has yielded no established treatment. Because the microbial layer and the salivary gland transcriptome or proteome have never been measured in the same patients, the model proposed here remains a testable hypothesis rather than a completed causal chain. The aim is to specify that model, the falsification conditions it carries, and the study design its verification requires.

papers.title: Integrative Molecular Profiling and Single-Cell Characterization of LHFPL5 Reveal Cancer-Specific Regulatory Features in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma and Lung Adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Al-Nakhle HH, Doha ZO.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives : LHFPL5 encodes a four-pass transmembrane protein essential for cochlear mechanotransduction, but its molecular behavior in cancer remains poorly defined. We characterized the genomic, epigenetic, transcriptomic, immune, and cellular context of LHFPL5 in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (KIRC) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), along with its associations with clinical outcomes. Materials and Methods : Retrospective analyses integrated TCGA RNA sequencing, clinical, DNA methylation, copy number, tumor purity, and immune deconvolution data. Transcriptome-wide associations and Hallmark enrichment defined LHFPL5 -associated programs. Continuous-expression Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) per standard-deviation increase, adjusted for age, sex, and pathological stage. GEO cohorts assessed external reproducibility, matched TCGA expression pipelines assessed processing sensitivity, and three non-TCGA single-cell datasets examined cellular localization. Results : LHFPL5 showed distinct molecular contexts in KIRC and LUAD. In KIRC, higher expression remained associated with poorer overall survival after clinical adjustment (528 patients; 174 deaths; HR = 1.36, 95% CI 1.21-1.53; p = 2.42 × 10 -7 ), while subtype and immune fractions showed limited statistical overlap with the association. In LUAD, expression covaried with copy-number state and showed a weak inverse relationship with first-exon methylation. Proliferation-related transcriptional programs were associated with survival, although enrichment support depended on the multiple-testing procedure. The primary STAR-derived LUAD analysis was null (485 patients; 177 deaths; HR = 1.02, 95% CI 0.89-1.18; p = 0.770), and survival inference varied with RNA processing. External adjusted replication was inconclusive. Single-cell detection was sparse in KIRC and one LUAD dataset; another LUAD cohort showed more frequent epithelial detection without resolved malignant-cell identity. Conclusions : LHFPL5 exhibits cancer-specific molecular architecture. LUAD showed copy-number, methylation, and proliferation-related associations, whereas KIRC showed a distinct molecular context with an independent survival signal. These findings support context-dependent LHFPL5 regulation and prioritize genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptional mechanisms for functional investigation.

papers.title: Identification and validation of biomarkers related to oxidative stress in pediatric sepsis utilizing WGCNA and multiple machine learning algorithms.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Luo G.
papers.abstract: Background This research aimed to identify novel oxidative stress (OS)-related biomarkers and develop predictive models for the early detection of pediatric sepsis. Methods Five open-access datasets from the gene expression omnibus database were analyzed, which included peripheral whole blood samples from children with sepsis and healthy controls. Using bioinformatics approaches, we identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with OS. We then combined weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and multiple machine learning algorithms (ML) to identify seven candidate genes, constructed a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network to screen six hub genes, and evaluated their correlations with the immune microenvironment. We subsequently evaluated the diagnostic performance of the hub genes using training datasets (GSE26440 and GSE26378) and validation datasets (GSE13904, GSE8121, and GSE9692). Moreover, molecular docking analysis revealed interactions between hub gene-encoded proteins and small-molecule compounds, which helps predict drug sensitivity. Results The study identified 36 differentially expressed oxidative stress-related genes (OSRGs). Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses highlighted these genes' roles in regulating inflammatory responses and reactive oxygen species metabolism. Seven candidate genes were identified using machine learning algorithms. Subsequently, through protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, six hub genes, namely, GADD45A, HP, MAPK14, PGD, RETN, and S100A9, were identified as having significant diagnostic potential. Immune cell deconvolution analysis of peripheral blood transcriptomes suggested that hub genes related to oxidative stress may be linked to alterations in the composition of peripheral blood immune cells. The diagnostic performance of the six hub genes was validated with area under the curve (AUC) values between 0.908 and 0.982, showing their promising diagnostic performance. Additionally, molecular docking analysis suggested that small molecules Doxycycline, Ralimetinib mesylate, Tasquinimod might interact with the identified hub genes, which opens up new treatment options. Conclusion Our research not only reveals potential diagnostic biomarkers of pediatric sepsis but also sets the stage for future studies. These studies aim to translate our findings into clinical practice, enabling earlier and more accurate diagnoses as well as targeted therapies to improve outcomes for children.

papers.title: Machine learning-based identification of CXCL13 and CXCL10 as key biomarkers in rheumatoid arthritis.
papers.authors: M S, S SA, M S, P N, Salau AO, Usman AG, Yousfan M.
papers.abstract: Background Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the autoimmune diseases that involve joint damage and synovial membrane inflammation. There have been many attempts to examine the utility of biomarkers in the diagnosis of RA, but there is no clinically accepted biomarker for the diagnosis of RA due to its heterogeneity. Thus, in this study, we tried to find RA biomarkers using machine learning and bioinformatics approaches. Methods Three corresponding gene expression datasets (GSE55457, GSE12021, and GSE77298) were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Batch effect correction was carried out using the ComBat function of the sva package in R. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) compared to controls were identified using limma . To identify the biological functions and pathways of DEGs, Gene Ontology, KEGG, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) were conducted. The protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed in Cytoscape using the STRING database. Genes identified through PPI analysis and further filtered by LASSO and SVM-RFE regressions were considered as diagnostic biomarkers. Additional analysis of hub genes was conducted using the GSE89408 dataset. CIBERSORTx was used to evaluate the immune cell infiltration in RA. Results A total of 440 DEGs were selected, including 197 downregulated and 243 upregulated genes. The DEGs were involved in biological processes and pathways associated with the immune system and were suggested by functional enrichment analysis. GSEA enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, hematopoietic cell lineage, primary immunodeficiency, and RA pathways. The hub genes CXCL13 and CXCL10 were chosen with the help of a machine learning algorithm. An external independent validation of the hub genes was conducted. In addition, ROC analysis showed a good diagnostic value of the two genes. The analysis of immune cell infiltration showed CXCL13 was associated with multiple immune-cell populations, including plasma cells, T-cell subsets, and M1 macrophages, whereas CXCL10 showed significant associations with M1 macrophages, plasma cells, and selected T-cell subsets. Correlation analysis showed a high correlation between chemokines CXCL13 and CXCL10 and many infiltrated immune cells. Conclusion The present study indicates the potential usefulness of CXCL13 and CXCL10 genes as diagnostic biomarkers in RA. Synovial inflammation in RA is associated with the coordinated action of many genes involved in the recruitment of various immune cells to the inflammatory site. Although the term chemokines were used to designate them, these genes are the genes encoding molecules associated with the migration of particular immune cell types, and CXCR5 and CXCR3 may be considered the potential targets for future research.

papers.title: Development of REC1: A Reverse Vaccinology-Derived Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Brucellosis.
papers.authors: Liu S, Dai Y, Huang F, Gao Z, Chen Z, Long M, Li S.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives : Brucellosis is a widespread intracellular zoonosis that continues to impose substantial public-health and economic burdens in endemic regions. No human brucellosis vaccine has yet been approved, and most existing multi-epitope candidates rely solely on computational predictions, without population-specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) optimization or in vivo epitope validation. REC1 is therefore an early-stage, proof-of-concept, human-oriented multi-epitope candidate, with epitopes screened against high-frequency HLA alleles in the Chinese population. This study developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate, REC1, using an integrated reverse-vaccinology workflow. Methods : We predicted Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) I and II epitopes against high-frequency HLA alleles representative of the Chinese population (AFND). Population coverage of the final incorporated epitope set was estimated with the IEDB Population Coverage tool under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, while paired HLA-DQ heterodimers, which the tool cannot model, were evaluated independently from Chinese DQA1-DQB1 haplotype frequencies. Epitopes supported by in vivo immunoreactivity were then assembled into the modular REC1 construct, which we characterized in silico for physicochemical properties, structural architecture, and simulated immune responses. Results : IFN-γ ELISpot shortlisted seven MHC-I and five MHC-II candidate immunoreactive epitopes derived from five Brucella antigens, of which five MHC-I and five MHC-II (one per antigen) were incorporated into REC1. The incorporated set was predicted to cover 91.17% of the China Oriental population on a conservative class I+II estimate (98.88% when HLA-DP was included; the HLA-DQ component alone covered 58-79%, 68.17% in Han). Epitope-level BLAST showed that all twelve shortlisted epitopes were 100% conserved across major Brucella species, except that the two Omp31 epitopes are absent from the Omp31-deleted B. abortus . The 35.86 kDa REC1 construct was predicted to be highly stable (instability index = 25.25) and hydrophilic, with a distinct architecture in which the carrier domain is ordered and the epitope region is disordered. Immune simulations suggested that REC1 can induce Th1-polarized humoral and cellular responses and may support long-term immunological memory. Molecular docking predicted that the L7/L12 carrier forms well-defined interfaces with TLR2, CD14, C1q, and DC-SIGN, and a representative peptide-MHC model confirmed canonical groove binding of a CTL epitope. Conclusions : REC1 exhibits favorable in silico properties, and its embedded peptides show IFN-γ immunogenicity in mice (candidate immunoreactive epitopes), lending preliminary support to its value as a multi-epitope vaccine candidate. HLA-matched validation and challenge studies are still needed to establish protective efficacy. Our study also offers a validated reverse vaccinology framework for future brucellosis vaccine development.

papers.title: House dust mite drives biphasic immunomodulation of inflammatory dendritic epidermal cells via glucose metabolism in atopic dermatitis.
papers.authors: Zhao Y, Gao C, Sui X, Ge L, Wang H, Deng S, Chen Q, Liu L, Tian J, Mu T, Wang L, Song Z.
papers.abstract: Background The impact of environmental antigens, specifically house dust mite (HDM) and Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin B (SEB), on the metabolism of inflammatory dendritic epidermal cells (IDECs) and its role in atopic dermatitis (AD) pathogenesis is poorly understood. This study aimed to characterize IDECs metabolism in AD and study how antigen exposure drives metabolic reprogramming and immune responses. Methods We first analyzed the single-cell RNA transcriptome sequencing data to explore metabolic profiles in IDECs from AD patients. Subsequently, we evaluated the effects of HDM alone or in combination with SEB for 24 h on the energy metabolism, maturation and cytokines secretion of monocytes-derived IDECs (moIDECs) in vitro . Finally, we investigated the dynamic changes of functional and glucose metabolism in moIDECs in vitro treated with HDM at different time points (6 h, 24 h, 48 h, 72 h). Results In AD skin lesions, inflammation- and metabolism-related genes of IDECs are abnormally expressed, and multiple metabolic pathways, including glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, are significantly dysregulated. HDM alone or in combination with SEB activated the glycolysis, induced the upregulation of maturation markers (CD80/83/86) of moIDECs in vitro , and promoted the production of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-23, IL-10, IL-12 and TNF-α), whereas SEB alone showed no significant effect. Furthermore, we found that HDM dynamically regulated inflammatory immune response of moIDECs. In the early phase (6-24 h), a pro-inflammatory profile predominated, observed with peak levels of IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-18, IL-12, TNF-α and IL-23. This subsequently transitions into the late phase (48-72 h) characterized by an anti-inflammatory shift, marked by elevated IL-10, classical tolerogenic molecules (IDO1, PDL1, and ILT3), and a profile consistent with the potential to induce regulatory T cells (Tregs). Concurrently, metabolic adaptations were observed, with glycolysis peaking at 24 h. Conclusion HDM-driven AD progression is correlated with changes in glucose metabolism and a biphasic immune shift in IDECs. Targeting HDM-responsive metabolic pathways like glycolysis might offer novel therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Gut microbiota, microbial metabolites, and mucosal barrier dysfunction in benign anorectal disorders and ulcerative colitis: shared mechanisms, clinical links, and precision interventions.
papers.authors: Yuan H, Zhao M, Wang Y, Shen C, Liu D, Wang C, Liu J.
papers.abstract: Benign anorectal disorders and ulcerative colitis (UC) are typically managed as separate clinical conditions, despite growing recognition of overlapping pathophysiological features. Constipation, hemorrhoidal disease, anal fistula and colonic mucosal inflammation may converge on partially shared molecular pathways involving microbial dysbiosis, altered microbial metabolite generation, epithelial barrier impairment, immune activation, stromal remodeling and dysregulated tissue repair, although the strength of mechanistic evidence varies substantially among these conditions. This review synthesizes advances from the past decade to propose a translational molecular medicine framework for investigating potential molecular connections among anatomically distinct anorectal and colonic disorders, without assuming shared causal origins. Clinical and pathological associations between disordered defecation, hemorrhoidal vascular remodeling, fistula persistence and UC are contextualized alongside current insights into gut and anorectal microbiota dysbiosis, short-chain fatty acid signaling, bile acid metabolism, tryptophan metabolite activity, gas-producing microbial communities, mucus biology, tight junction function, innate and adaptive immune responses, and fibro-inflammatory repair processes. Integrating microbiome profiling, metabolomics, transcriptomics, single-cell and spatial analyses with causal inference provides a cross-disease framework for resolving convergent molecular states associated with recurrence, healing and therapeutic response. By moving beyond disease-by-disease description, this strategy may uncover biomarkers and actionable pathways otherwise overlooked, supporting mechanism-informed prevention, perioperative optimization and individualized intervention across anorectal disorders and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

papers.title: Baseline growth kinetics of pulmonary metastases in head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma: analysis of correlated clinical and molecular factors.
papers.authors: Liu HF, Jiang LY, Ma TY, Zhao Y, Li TY, Wang XL, Zhang SJ, Yang GL, Zhou J, Yan ZY, Chen XH.
papers.abstract: Objective To establish baseline growth rates of lung nodules in untreated head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma(ACC) patients and analyze associated clinical and molecular factors influencing these rates. Methods CT was used to calculate the diameter of 74 pulmonary metastatic nodules in 37 patients under natural state. The diameter growth rate of lung metastatic nodules was fitted with a linear regression equation, and the differences in the progression rate of lung metastasis among patients were compared. Additionally, clinical features such as location, pathological subtypes, and staging were also collected to compare their correlation with the growth rate of lung metastatic nodules. Subsequently, single-cell sequencing data from three lung metastatic nodules of differing diameters within the same case were analyzed. Results We defined three different states based on the progression of lung metastases: rapid progression was defined as a monthly diameter increase of more than 1 mm in 16.2% (6/37) of the patients; slow progression was defined as a monthly diameter increase between 0.3-1 mm in 56.8% (21/37) of the patients; and stable state was defined as a monthly diameter increase of less than 0.3 mm in 27.0% (10/37) of the patients. In addition, factors such as low expression of TP63, a higher pathological grade (Grade III), and a nodule diameter greater than 10mm at initial diagnosis of lung metastasis were identified as significant predictors for a faster diameter growth rate (P Conclusion The findings of this study suggest that baseline characteristics based on the growth rate of pulmonary metastatic nodules may be used to help stratify the progression rate of lung metastasis. In particular, based on our observations, for patients with pulmonary metastatic lesions presenting with a nodule diameter > 10 mm, pathological grade III, and low TP63 expression at initial diagnosis, clinicians might consider adopting closer follow-up monitoring or potentially initiating intervention measures earlier. Additionally, for rapidly growing pulmonary metastatic nodules, it may be worth considering targeted therapy against hypoxic/anti-angiogenic pathways or combination with immunotherapy aimed at restoring or enhancing local immune responses.

papers.title: Whole-Genome Resequencing Reveals Genomic Signatures Underlying High-Altitude Adaptation in Ethiopian Indigenous Cattle.
papers.authors: Ma R, Li D, Lu Y, Wang B, Deng W, Gao Z.
papers.abstract: High-altitude environments impose severe physiological challenges on mammals, yet the genetic basis of adaptation in Ethiopian indigenous cattle remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed whole-genome resequencing data from 70 Ethiopian indigenous cattle representing seven breeds (Abigar, Barka, Boran, Felata, Fogera, Gojjam-Highland, and Horro) distributed across elevations ranging from 523 to 3410 m, obtained from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive. After alignment to the ARS-UCD2.0 reference genome, we identified 49,196,624 high-confidence SNPs and performed population genomic analyses (PCA, phylogenetic reconstruction, and ADMIXTURE), along with genome-wide selection scans using FST and nucleotide diversity (θπ), and in silico virtual knockout of candidate genes in bovine lung single-cell transcriptomics. Population structure analyses revealed marked genetic differentiation between low- and mid-to-high-altitude populations, with substantial genetic connectivity and shared ancestry among high-altitude groups. We identified 398 candidate selective regions showing concordant FST and θπ signals, encompassing 1816 candidate genes, significantly enriched in hypoxia-related and vascular remodeling pathways (phospholipase D, Ras, ErbB, Wnt, Hedgehog). Two hub candidate genes, PIK3CA and RHOA , were prioritized; virtual perturbation of PIK3CA altered extracellular matrix, focal adhesion, and integrin networks, whereas RHOA perturbation activated immune and inflammatory programs (NF-κB, phagocytosis, chemokine pathways) with upregulation of TYROBP , IL1B , TLR4 , and NLRP3 . Our findings indicate that Ethiopian cattle have evolved distinct genomic signatures associated with adaptation to chronic high-altitude environments, in which PIK3CA and RHOA may represent candidate regulators associated with extracellular matrix organization and immune-related transcriptional regulation, respectively, thereby providing new insights into mammalian adaptation to extreme environments.

papers.title: Identification of CLOCK and MARK2 as Candidate Blood-Based Biomarkers in Type 2 Diabetes: An Integrated Bulk and Single-Cell Transcriptomic Study.
papers.authors: Yang L, Tang J, Zhang D, Yun P.
papers.abstract: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is often accompanied by nervous system complications. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying T2DM remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify candidate blood-based biomarkers associated with T2DM by screening a neural-related gene set through integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis of peripheral blood. The present analysis focused on the systemic expression patterns of the selected genes in peripheral blood as indicators of T2DM-associated immunometabolic dysregulation, rather than on neurological involvement. The neural-related gene set was used only as a predefined screening starting point. Methods: We employed a three-tier validation framework comprising (1) a training cohort (GSE15932, 8 T2DM patients vs. 8 controls) for biomarker discovery using differential expression analysis and machine learning (XGBoost, random forest, and PPI network topology); (2) an independent validation cohort (GSE184050, 50 T2DM patients vs. 65 controls) for cross-dataset diagnostic performance assessment (ROC analysis); and (3) an experimental validation cohort (5 T2DM patients vs. 5 controls) for independent clinical confirmation by RT-qPCR. Additionally, single-cell RNA sequencing (GSE268210) was used to investigate cell type-specific expression and immune regulatory networks. Results: By combining multiple screening methods and cross-dataset validation, we identified CLOCK and MARK2 as key candidate genes from the neural-related gene set. CLOCK and MARK2 showed high discriminatory performance in the discovery cohort, whereas their AUCs were 0.613 and 0.653, respectively, in the validation cohort, indicating limited standalone discriminatory ability. Both genes are highly expressed in peripheral blood monocytes and are associated with MIF-(CD74+CXCR4)-mediated cell communication, TNFA-NFκB inflammatory signaling, and activation of oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Finally, RT-qPCR in clinical samples confirmed that both genes were indeed upregulated ( p Conclusions: CLOCK and MARK2 were identified as candidate T2DM-associated blood-based biomarkers with reproducible expression differences across datasets. Their discriminatory performance was more modest in the independent validation cohort, indicating limited standalone diagnostic utility. Single-cell and computational analyses further suggested potential immunometabolic relevance. Because neurological phenotyping, cognitive assessment, and direct measures of nervous system involvement were not available in this study, any relationship between these genes and the neurological manifestations of T2DM remains speculative and hypothesis-generating, and requires prospective validation in cohorts with matched neurocognitive data.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Nanobody Engineering for Pathogen Recognition: From Functional Epitope Prioritization to Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.authors: Hu RS, Ehsan M, Luo W, Zhou J, Xiao YL, Wang HX, Li CY, Gu K.
papers.abstract: Nanobodies are compact and stable proteins derived from the variable domain of camelid heavy-chain-only antibodies (VHH). Advances in structural biology, molecular modeling, and artificial intelligence (AI) are shifting VHH discovery from empirical selection toward data-driven design. However, predicted binding alone does not ensure biological activity or successful translation, particularly for antigenically variable pathogens. Complementing recent reviews that broadly survey computational VHH modeling and optimization, this review focuses on how antigen biology and functional epitope prioritization can guide the design of pathogen-targeting VHHs. We organize the field along a structure-function-translation continuum, connecting the structural basis of VHH recognition and available data resources with conventional discovery, antigen-guided de novo design, and sequence-structure learning. We further examine how developability, recombinant production, multispecificity, humanization, structural dynamics, and antigenic variation shape the progression from predicted binders to functional VHHs. Finally, we discuss how multimodal foundation models could integrate these dimensions to support the design of functional, manufacturable, and escape-resilient VHHs.

papers.title: Metabolic Milieu and Susceptibility: The Combined Benefits of Targeting AMPK and ACE2 for Metabolic Disorders and COVID-19.
papers.authors: Tata FY, Nxumalo MB, Ntanzi N, Mushebenge AG, Khan RB, Kumalo HM.
papers.abstract: The convergence of metabolic dysfunction and infectious diseases has become increasingly evident, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) emerge as pivotal molecular regulators linking metabolic homeostasis, endothelial integrity, immune modulation, and viral pathogenesis. Metabolic diseases such as diabetes, obesity, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease are marked by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction, collectively increasing susceptibility to severe viral infections and outcomes. This review examines experimental, computational, and translational evidence exploring the interplay between AMPK and ACE2, focusing on metabolic, vascular, and inflammatory pathways relevant to viral infections. Recent findings show a bidirectional functional relationship between AMPK and ACE2, where AMPK phosphorylation supports ACE2 expression and function, and ACE2 signaling reciprocally enhances AMPK activity, forming a protective metabolic-vascular loop. Disruption of this axis, particularly through SARS-CoV-2-induced ACE2 degradation, exacerbates metabolic deterioration, vascular damage, and exaggerated inflammatory responses. Preclinical and in silico studies show that pharmacological AMPK activators, including metformin and bioactive flavonoids, demonstrate pleiotropic metabolic, anti-inflammatory, endothelial protective, and potential antiviral activities, hinting at the therapeutic potential of modulating the AMPK-ACE2 axis, despite the limited clinical application of flavonoids. The AMPK-ACE2 axis represents an important molecular link between metabolic regulation, renovascular health, and immune defense mechanisms. This evaluation connects AMPK and ACE2 from isolated signaling nodes into a coordinated pharmacological axis with implications for interventions in cardiometabolic and viral diseases. Future research should prioritize mechanistic validation and conduct integrated experimental and clinical investigations to establish AMPK-ACE2 co-targeting as a viable therapeutic strategy for mitigating cardiometabolic disease burden and enhancing resilience against viral infections.

papers.title: Beyond Histocompatibility: Donor Tissue Immune States and Their Role in Heart Transplantation.
papers.authors: Urbanowicz T, Kowalewski M, Suwalski P, Raffa GM.
papers.abstract: Heart transplantation transfers not only donor alloantigens and functional myocardium but also a pre-existing tissue environment shaped by resident immune, vascular, stromal, and parenchymal populations. This review examines the hypothesis that the biological state of donor tissue influences subsequent recipient immunity and contributes to heterogeneity in allograft outcomes. Donor-resident macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, and tissue-resident lymphocytes constitute an immunologically active myocardial niche that encounters ischemia-reperfusion injury and recipient immune effectors immediately after implantation. Experimental and human studies demonstrate the dynamic coexistence and replacement of donor- and recipient-derived immune populations, with recipient cells acquiring phenotypes within the graft microenvironment. We distinguish transient donor-tissue activation from genuine tissue immune memory, which would require persistence of an exposure-induced molecular or functional state and an altered response to a subsequent challenge. Potential mechanisms include trained innate immunity, epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, endothelial inflammatory memory, and persistent stromal-immune interactions. We propose that allograft biology be investigated at the level of the donor-recipient immune pair and outline longitudinal single-cell, spatial, and cell-of-origin approaches to test this concept in human heart transplantation.

papers.title: Genetic Susceptibility in Dry Eye Disease: Immunogenetic Evidence, Current Limitations, and Future Directions.
papers.authors: Capobianco M, Zeppieri M, Cappellani F, Gagliano C, Consoli RA, Mangiagli S, Roszkowska AM.
papers.abstract: Dry eye disease is a multifactorial disorder which is heterogeneous in nature, caused by interactions among ocular surface abnormalities, systemic diseases, environmental factors and host susceptibility. The inherited variation related to the pathophysiology of dry eye disease is not very well characterized, but known mechanisms include inflammation, tear film instability, neurosensory dysfunction and lacrimal and meibomian gland changes. Studies exploring the contribution of genetics suggest that dry eye disease (DED) and specific ocular surface endophenotypes are heritable. Candidate-gene and human leukocyte antigen association studies have reinforced contributions from pathways associated with innate and adaptive immunity, inflammatory regulation and neural function, and glandular homeostasis, but many associations require replication in larger, more diverse populations. Genome-wide association studies and biobank-based assessments have recently begun to shed light on the polygenic architecture of Dry Eye Disease (DED) and its genetic overlap with other related conditions worldwide. This paper evaluates critically the current evidence on DED heritability, candidate susceptibility genes, HLA associations, genome-wide signals, polygenic risk models and genetic pleiotropy. It will cover how transcriptomic, epigenomic, and single-cell approaches can link inherited susceptibility loci to disease-relevant cell states and molecular pathways across the ocular surface unit, including the cornea, conjunctiva, lacrimal gland, and meibomian glands. The study would stress phenotypic heterogeneity, ancestry-related limitations, and inconsistent diagnostic definitions. In the end, we will evaluate opportunities and existing constraints in the incorporation of genomic information with clinical endophenotypes and environmental exposures to support risk stratification, biomarker discovery, identification of therapeutic targets, and the development of future ocular surface precision medicine.

papers.title: Identification and In Vitro Validation of Metabolic Reprogramming-Related Hub Genes for the Diagnosis of Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
papers.authors: Xue J, Zhang Z, Wei W, Zhang A, Zhou X, Wu Q, Chen S, Deng J, Zhang X.
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolic reprogramming plays a vital role in subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). This study aims to identify biomarkers related to metabolic reprogramming in SAH. Methods: Transcriptome datasets (GSE36791 and GSE73378) were downloaded from the GEO database, and the metabolic reprogramming-related genes were retrieved from the Molecular Signatures Database. Candidate genes were identified by intersecting differentially expressed genes, WGCNA module genes, and metabolic genes. Hub genes were screened via CytoHubba, machine learning, and Mendelian randomization. ROC curves were generated to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the hub genes. Additionally, functional enrichment analysis, circulating immune-cell composition analysis, and drug prediction were performed. A cellular SAH model (U251 cells) and clinical samples were used for RT-qPCR validation.
